title: The software engineering hiring rebound has a catch: It's leaving early-career engineers behind
description: Software engineer job postings are rising again, but early-career workers aren't seeing the same recovery.
fullText:
Software engineering hiring is rebounding, but not all workers appear to be sharing in the recovery.

Nearly 70% of software development postings were for senior-level roles, per recent Indeed data.

The AI boom may favor experienced engineers who can direct AI tools and review their work.

After years of layoffs, businesses are hiring more software engineers — but the rebound is spread unevenly.

As of the first quarter of this year, nearly 70% of US software development job postings on Indeed were for senior-level roles, rather than mid- or entry-level. That's up from 55% in early 2019.

Of the more than 40 employment sectors that Indeed analyzed across the economy, software development had the highest share of senior-level postings.

As AI reshapes the economy, software engineering has become a closely watched test case for what the technology could mean for workers. After surging during the early pandemic years, software development job postings began to plummet in 2022. The downturn overlapped with the release of ChatGPT and other AI models, raising questions about whether AI was reducing demand for software engineers.

But over the past year and a half, the trend has started to reverse. Software development postings remain below pre-pandemic levels, but were up roughly 15% in June from early 2025.

In Indeed's analysis, senior engineers appear to be finding their footing in the age of AI, while less-experienced engineers aren't seeing the same recovery.

Sneha Puri, economist at Indeed Hiring Lab, said the recent rebound in software development postings has been tied in part to a return to more normal hiring levels in the tech sector after years of slower hiring.

But she said perhaps the likeliest explanation for the uptick is that companies still need people to direct AI tools and review the code they churn out, especially for more complex projects. That need tends to favor senior engineers.

"AI tools can increasingly handle the routine, well-defined coding tasks that used to be assigned to junior engineers," she said. "That shifts hiring demand toward workers who can direct AI output, catch its mistakes, and make the judgment calls AI can't — skills that typically come with experience."

Some software engineers say they've seen that shift firsthand.

Manoj Aggarwal, a software engineer with more than a decade of experience, said he noticed more openings for senior engineering roles than junior ones during a job search last year. In his current role, Aggarwal said AI has transformed his workflow, with much of his coding time now spent prompting AI tools and reviewing their output.

title: SEE IT: Puerto Ricans reject 51st state push as residents fear taxes could skyrocket
description: Puerto Ricans told Fox News Digital they fear statehood would spike taxes and threaten the island's cultural identity amid its ongoing debt crisis.
fullText:
Several Puerto Ricans interviewed by Fox News Digital in San Juan, Puerto Rico voiced opposition to becoming America's 51st state, arguing that it would send the economy into turmoil and strip the island of its cultural identity.

"I don't think it should be a state," Carly, who grew up in Puerto Rico and now lives in Connecticut, told Fox News Digital. "I don't want them to do PR how they did with Hawaii. I don't want taxes to spike. People's wages here are really low to maintain life here."

Statehood for Puerto Rico, a U.S. territory since the United States acquired it from Spain in 1898, has long been debated among both the U.S. government and Puerto Rico's local government.

Caribbean Hot Spot Gripped By Water Crisis, And Tourists Scramble To Reschedule Plans

The statehood debate carries significant economic implications for the island, including potential changes to how Puerto Rican residents and businesses are taxed. Puerto Rico operates under a different federal tax structure than the states — statehood would bring the island more fully into the federal tax system.

"Everything would become more expensive than it already is and locals [have] already been struggling for a while now," Alejandra from San Juan, Puerto Rico, said. She continued, "It would make stuff even worse."

Puerto Rican Gov. Jenniffer González Colón, a member of the pro-statehood New Progressive Party and ally of President Donald Trump, is an advocate of the push for Puerto Rico to become the 51st state. She argues that achieving statehood goes hand-in-hand with achieving equality, as her party has claimed unequal treatment in numerous federal programs.

Puerto Rico Governor Signs Law Recognizing Unborn Babies As Human Beings

One Puerto Rican resident who spoke with Fox News Digital cited the public scrutiny of Trump as a reason for not wanting to gain statehood. Although Puerto Ricans are U.S. citizens, residents of the territory cannot vote in the general election for president.

"There's a lot of controversy with the… especially the president right now," a woman from Puerto Rico who referred to herself as "Boo" said. "We don't want to be a part of that, for sure."

A nonbinding referendum on the issue held in November 2024 asked Puerto Rican voters to choose between statehood, independence or associated independence — which leaves certain issues to be negotiated individually. The vote found that 59% of those voting were in favor of statehood, with 29% favoring independence and 12% for associated independence.

"I believe that we can be our own independent country," Angelie, another Puerto Rican resident, said. "I think that we have the full potential to become an independent country since we have been colonized for so, so many years."

She continued, "We had the chance to be a country then the United States, no hate though, colonized us and promised us something and then it was another stuff."

Another resident expressed his support for Puerto Rico gaining independence, but said it's "not ready for that."

"I truly believe that Puerto Rico should be part of the nations around the world as an independent nation like the U.S. is," Luis from Puerto Rico said.

Carville Tells Dems To Quietly Prepare Power Grab With Dc, Puerto Rico Statehood And Supreme Court Packing

Luis also cited Puerto Rico's economic relationship with the federal government as one reason he questions whether the island is prepared for independence.

"The reality is that we have been… tailored to the U.S. — not citizens, the U.S. government, federal government — to their liking," Luis said. "In other words, they have been feeding us with a lot of federal funding and people are used to that."

He continued, "A lot of people do not work just because they are used to get the federal funds. So that's a shame."

In addition to the economic concerns presented, "Boo" pointed to her fear that Puerto Rico would lose its culture if it joined the U.S. as a state.

"Puerto Rico is already being very Americanized," she said. "I wouldn't like that to keep going on if we become a state because it will lose the heart and soul."

Aug 24 (Reuters) - Iran said it had blacklisted 45 tankers that had broken its rules for crossing the Strait of Hormuz, and would take action against any ‌vessels transferring loads with them, escalating its threats over the key waterway six months into the war.

The ‌named vessels could be fined, detained and have their cargoes confiscated, according to an X post late on Sunday from the Persian Gulf Strait ​Authority, a new body set up by Iran to manage the strait.

The warning was issued within days of the U.S. threatening Iran with "the toughest sanctions in history", and Iran saying its response to any new U.S. threats would be "devastating".

The restricted list includes very large crude carriers, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, and clean product vessels, among others.

Some ‌of the named ships are owned by ⁠the United Arab Emirates' ADNOC Logistics and Shipping (ADNOC L&S), ADNOC's subsidiary Navig8 Tankers, and Saudi Arabia's national shipping carrier Bahri.

Trump admin celebrated the prosecution of accused MS-13 ringleaders. Then the case fell apart twice
description: The Trump administration celebrated the arrival of an alleged MS-13 mastermind on American soil in March 2025.
fullText:
The Trump administration celebrated the arrival of an alleged MS-13 mastermind on American soil in March 2025.

But it was Moises Rivera-Luna — a man whom the Justice Department says ordered murders in the US from inside a Salvadoran jail cell more than a decade ago — who fell to his knees, stunned and grateful, in a Washington, DC, courtroom this April.

It was the second time in five months the Justice Department had tried him before a federal jury. And for the second time, his jury failed to reach a verdict.

Portrayed as a brutal gang leader known as "Viejo Santos," or "Old Saint," Rivera-Luna was squarely among the types of criminal defendants President Donald Trump and, by extension, DC US Attorney Jeanine Pirro, has most sought to convict. But over the past year, the case against Rivera-Luna has run up against two juries in Washington that simply couldn't agree, ending both rounds of the Justice Department's efforts in mistrials.

"I've done this a long time and haven't seen one quite like this one," Judge Royce Lamberth, who's been on the bench for nearly 40 years, said as the second trial neared its deadlocked end.

It's unclear exactly what broke down during jury deliberations in both trials.

The arc of this case, though, has become unusually commonplace in the federal court in Washington this year.

Pirro's office has secured some convictions at trial in federal court, and touted several successful prosecutions of violent crime in Washington's local Superior Court.

Yet Pirro's office has a jury problem. An increasingly alarming number of cases have fallen apart this year in DC's federal court — even when the cases appear to be strong arguments against violent crime, relatively straightforward to prove, and tried by experienced prosecutors.

Before the MS-13 case was re-tried in April, the DC US Attorney's Office had secured convictions in only four of the eight federal cases tried before Washington juries since January.

Since the MS-13 case's jury hung in April, the US Attorney's Office has tried nearly a dozen more criminal cases in DC's federal court.

In two, the defendants were acquitted. Four of the trials ended in deadlock, with jurors reporting in courtroom notes that they deliberated "hopelessly" and were in complete "impasse." Mistrials were declared.

That track record for the US Attorney's Office is essentially unheard of in recent memory, according to over two dozen Washington, DC, investigators, former prosecutors, defense attorneys and other legal experts. Many of the people in the legal community asked not to be named because they practice in the DC federal courthouse or have ties to the US attorney's office.

Federal juries typically decide to convict defendants in criminal trials nationwide at a rate of about 90%, according to federal judiciary statistics.

Several people in Washington's legal community who've interacted with federal jurors say perhaps the juries are politically unhappy with the Trump administration and, thus, take issue with the Justice Department.

But in cases like MS-13, the jurors simply appear to be more closely scrutinizing the cases presented to them by the Justice Department, many of the legal community sources say.

"This is not a political case. I think this is a failure of proof and a stubbornness born of desperation on the part of the prosecutors' office," Robert Feitel, who is one of two lawyers representing one of the MS-13 defendants, told CNN recently.

While each case at trial where Pirro's office has struggled to convict is different, several of the people in the legal community have called the trend with the DC juries in federal court "embarrassing" or described it as dire. The cases — some being retried weeks or months later — are bogging down a US attorney's office that has already been stretched thin with Trump-prompted firings and departures and sullied by Pirro's political missteps in cases the president has wanted.

Many fear how even the office's most experienced prosecutors might fare in trials set for the coming months. That includes the trial to begin this week for an alleged conspirator in the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland.

At very least, the MS-13 case has become the portrait of the unpredictability of Washington, DC, juries.

"It's just the wheels of justice rolling along," Christopher Davis, the defense attorney of a cooperating witness in the MS-13 case, told CNN during the April trial.

"DC juries tend to lean left, and they're highly educated," Davis said. "They take their job seriously. They overturn every stone."

The MS-13 case grappled with severe violence in the community, putting on trial five murders or assaults the Justice Department says were prompted by the orders of gang leaders years ago. The top defendant was Rivera-Luna, a stone-faced alleged mastermind who wore glasses every day in court and politely interacted with his lawyer in Spanish. Guatemalan authorities had apprehended him, sending him to the US in custody last year.

Prosecutors say Rivera-Luna was at the top of the gang hierarchy when MS-13 members carried out several shootings and stabbings of their peers in the DC area who breached the organization's codes from 2008 to 2010.

One of the victims had shifted a knife he had between his pockets at a gang meeting, breaking a rule of the brotherhood, at a park just outside DC. A few days later the man had been lured into the woods, shot and left to die. Another riding a bicycle while wearing a red bandana was perceived as a rival and gunned down by MS-13 members, prosecutors say.

Rivera-Luna was recorded on phone calls in those years speaking to a man in the DC area — whom years later has become one of the trial witnesses against him — from inside a Latin American prison.

Both juries at the two trials heard the audio of Rivera-Luna telling the MS-13 contact, in Spanish, "You have 13 days to eat chicken," the prosecutor said.

"He was giving me 13 days to kill someone," the witness testified later about that call.

Rivera-Luna's trial co-defendant, Tokiro Rodas Ramirez, had been picked up by authorities in Honduras' capital city during a soccer game in 2022. Now in the US in custody, the latter defendant is tall and broad-shouldered, and expressive in the courtroom, smiling regularly at jurors and others watching the case. His nickname within MS-13, according to court records, was "Perverso," and he had been a local leader of the gang in the DC region when the assaults took place, prosecutors alleged.

Lamberth, who has presided over the conspiracy case since 2013, ushered the two men over the past year swiftly toward a first trial in December 2025.

The case's longtime lead prosecutor Nihar Mohanty and others from the DC US Attorney's Office had previously won jury convictions of co-conspirators at trial in 2013. The Justice Department also secured a string of guilty pleas and cooperation from others.

"These cases come with a playbook," the witness' attorney Davis, who has tried nearly a dozen similar MS-13 conspiracy cases, said. "It's hard to screw up these cases" from the government's perspective.

The December trial jury began deliberations after nine trial days and hearing from 22 witnesses called by the Justice Department. Initially, the December jury told Lamberth in a note they were close to unanimity on at least one of the three charges.

Then another morning of deliberation passed. Another note to the judge arrived. Any consensus had fallen apart, the jury said, indicating one juror refused to be impartial and continue deliberating with the others.

Lamberth drew out from that juror that he believed the deliberations had broken down into bullying.

"I feel like I have made my point that I have come to a final decision many times," the holdout juror, who has not been identified publicly, told the judge, according to a court transcript. "And then it just seems like it's an organized attack of over and over and over the same questions."

The man said he had broken down crying in the jury room.

Pirro, when asked by CNN about how the trial in December resulted in a hung jury, matter-of-factly said Mohanty and other prosecutors would just need to try the case again.

"We'll do whatever it takes within the bounds of the law to bring the guilty to justice. Whatever it takes," Pirro said. "And you know what? I have great prosecutors on that case, and I think that that (jury) note speaks for itself."

Mohanty delivered a nearly identical opening statement to this second jury in April as he did at the December trial.

One rule of the gang, Mohanty explained in his opening, was "kill rival gang members at every opportunity" and "greenlight," or kill, MS-13 members that didn't follow the gang's rules.

The defense lawyers insisted to the jury that their client's affiliation with MS-13 or their gang tattoos weren't proof of criminality.

The jury said in a note they couldn't agree to two of three criminal counts.

"We are not in agreement and some jurors have expressed they are firm in their votes … We are unsure of how to move forward. We have confirmed that even after further review and continued discussion these jurors are adamant this will not change their vote."

Lamberth, beginning to show his frustration, refused to call a mistrial.

The jurors returned Friday morning, April 17, to continue deliberations. They said nothing from the jury room to the judge nearly all day.

At 4 p.m., Lamberth's deputy called the prosecutors and the two defendants' defense lawyers back into the courtroom to see printouts of a new and more confusing note from the jury.

"We have reached a verdict on one count; however, discussions have once again stalled. We have one juror who has repeatedly stated they are firm on their decisions. This particular juror also stated on the first day that they are comfortable not reaching a consensus," the jury foreperson wrote. "We are unsure how to move forward, as it does not appear we will reach a consensus."

Rivera-Luna's lawyer, Alfred Guillaume, a typically dapper and relaxed attorney with a pocket square, read it over several times. Rodas Ramirez's attorney Feitel, more prone to fidgeting, paced around the courtroom, popping mints in his mouth.

The defense lawyers asked Lamberth to accept a partial verdict. That would likely bring to an end the 15-year-old case.

The defense lawyers huddled in the corner of the court room, trying to plot what to do next.

Mohanty, sitting at the top of the prosecutors' table, hung his head in his hand, rubbing his temples.

The court would need more time to decide what to do and Lamberth sent the jurors and the lawyers home for the weekend.

A cheer erupted from the jury room when the final of the 12 jurors arrived late Monday morning, April 20, to try again with deliberations.

They sent a note, however, 15 minutes later. A courtroom deputy read the jury's message aloud to the lawyers in the courtroom: "We discussed as a jury and no longer have consensus on the count we had previously reached a verdict on."

"This is the case that will never die," Guillaume responded.

"I suppose the good news is I'll get to see you again, Your Honor," Mohanty, the prosecutor, said.

After Lamberth declared the mistrial, the prosecutors and defense attorneys went to talk with the jurors about what happened.

All 12 jurors from the April trial declined to speak to CNN as they exited. But those in touch with them reported they appeared to be genuinely unable to reach a conclusion, even after having sketched out extensive notes in the jury room on white boards. They had appeared to gel as a group, with some bringing tulips and cupcakes to court on the final day.

"I was encouraged by how seriously they took their job," Guillaume said as he was leaving the courthouse.

But would he want to try this case again, I asked. "It's my job. I gotta try this case," he said, clearly frustrated and shaking his head.

The case against the two alleged MS-13 leaders is set to be retried again, for a third time, beginning in mid-September.

title: Rumours swirled after a Vietnamese teen was run over - then came a stunning admission
description: Confirmation of the circumstances around Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's death have only spurred more questions.
fullText:
Until recently, there would have been little to distinguish Vietnam's so-called Justice Tree from the hundreds of others lining the streets of Hanoi. Then the bouquets started piling up.

It was here that former politician Nguyen Sy Cuong was driving his BMW in May last year when he veered into the opposite lane and smashed into a motorbike carrying a father and his teenage daughter.

The father, Do Viet Hung, suffered a broken leg but survived. The daughter, 18-year-old Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy, died in hospital 10 days after the collision, which severed her right leg.

Fifteen months later, her death and the silence surrounding it has become a lightning rod for discontent among Vietnam's youth.

In early August, a legion of anonymous social media users started publishing millions of posts with the hashtags #NguyenSyCuong and #BMW across Facebook, Instagram, Threads and X. The users identified themselves as Gen Z – and they demanded accountability.

Initial discussions circled around whether the former politician was in fact the one who had caused the accident, and why authorities had only released sparse information.

Some pointed to reports that the driver of the BMW had the initials NSC and was born in 1961, leading to speculation that he was a former member of parliament. Others claimed the incident had been swept under the rug due to the influence of powerful figures.

Many reported that their posts had been deleted by social media platforms at the request of the Vietnamese government – providing screenshots of notifications as evidence. These claims could not be independently verified.

Expressions of outrage and calls for a proper investigation grew in number, volume and force.

Meanwhile, masked flower bearers started to appear, gravitating towards the scene of the incident and laying vibrant bouquets at the base of what has now been dubbed the Justice Tree. Police quickly arrived to get rid of the flowers, prompting mourners to create a virtual equivalent of the tree online - where hundreds of thousands of people have since sent tributes and paid respects.

Pressurised by more than a year's worth of growing suspicion and a rush of online attention, the issue had become too big to ignore.

Then, last Monday, the government made an extraordinary admission.

State broadcaster Vietnam Television (VTV) televised an official statement from authorities, confirming what had happened on the day of the incident. Former National Assembly deputy Nguyen Sy Cuong was indeed driving his car down Nguyen Huy Tu Street on 30 May, 2025, when his vehicle suddenly swerved across the road and into an oncoming motorcycle.

VTV cited police and prosecution sources who said that because Nguyen Sy Cuong "sincerely confessed and actively and fully remedied the consequences of his actions", Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's family had submitted a petition to exempt him from prosecution. The report did not specify what form this remedy took, but Nguyen Sy Cuong was cleared of all criminal liability.

While such a decision is lawful under Vietnam's legislation, lawyers have questioned whether the criminal proceedings were conducted in accordance with due process – or conducted at all. Social media users were quick to highlight his political connections and call for a more thorough investigation.

Such online pressure had yielded results in the past.

In March this year, a 66-year-old man driving under the influence of alcohol in Hanoi collided with seven other cars and three motorcycles in a chain-reaction crash that killed one woman and seriously injured two others.

In the wake of that incident, it emerged that the driver, Nguyen Van Sau, was a retired police colonel who had previously served as deputy director of a department under the Ministry of Public Security. Fearing that the driver was not being held culpable, the victim's family appealed for help. Social media users in turn amplified the issue, and after three months Nguyen Van Sau was charged with "violating regulations on participation in road traffic".

Who is To Lam, the ex-cop who wants to revamp Vietnam's success story?

British teen dies in reported Vietnam motorbike fall

Jailed Vietnamese tycoon's Birkin bags sell for more than $550K

Many now feel that a similar groundswell may be the only way to deliver justice for the teenager who died last year. But their efforts have been met with friction.

Do Viet Hung, the teenager's father, appeared in VTV's broadcast to thank internet users for their sympathy, but said the family was satisfied with the investigation's findings, and asked people to leave them alone. Notably, he also warned people "not to be drawn into the influence of reactionary elements".

Also appearing in the broadcast was a senior police official, who suggested that people were leveraging the incident to stoke dissent.

The Ministry of Public Security had "uncovered highly dangerous plots and intentions by hostile forces, reactionaries and bad actors to incite unrest and cause disorder", the official said.

"The ministry advises the public, especially young people, to remain fully alert and highly vigilant."

Similar rebukes have also started emerging on social media, with some claiming that conspiratorial forces were manipulating young people in Vietnam to stoke political discontent, manipulate public opinion online and rally people in real life ahead of the country's national holiday on 2 September.

Others have accused Gen Z Vietnamese of plotting a "colour revolution" – a term used to refer to mostly nonviolent protest movements that use specific colours or flowers as their symbol.

This is a familiar line of critique from Vietnamese authorities, who have previously labelled people's grievances or resentments as being untrue, unreasonable, or stemming from information fabricated by some "anti-government" or "reactionary" organisation.

Many in this case have said such accusations are baseless, insisting they are simply seeking justice for the victim of a fatal traffic accident. But the growing outrage has inevitably become a flashpoint amid broader, simmering grievances felt by Vietnam's youth.

Despite the Vietnamese government's tightening control over people's online freedom of expression – through measures ranging from intimidation and fines to criminal prosecution – public opinion in some corners has started to swerve against the Communist Party line.

On platforms such as Threads and Reddit, where anonymity is more normalised, many young people have expressed discontent towards various social issues: from the expansion of police power and land reclamation projects to exam cheating scandals and stricter regulation of online communication.

Such grievances echo those condemned by other Gen Z-led movements across the broader Asia region.

In countries like Bangladesh, India and Nepal, youth-led anti-government uprisings have over the past 12 months rallied immense support against the various pressure points of corruption, nepotism, economic inequality and democratic backsliding. Unofficially dubbed "the Asian Spring", the expanding influence of these movements has spread from Iran, Mongolia and the Maldives to the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

But protests in Vietnam have rarely, if ever, reached such fierce extremes. Vietnamese authorities have historically proven effective at detecting and stifling dissent before it boils over into action. Virtual places of mourning, anonymous social media posts, and online protests seem to be the most strident action many civilians here can afford to take.

Many are simply seeking justice for a teenager who was killed in a tragic accident, and accountability for a former lawmaker who appears to have been granted special clemency.

Yet even the mere suggestion that this incident could foment an uprising has provoked alarm – along with harsh reminders of the longstanding status quo in Vietnam's one-party state.

"Are these Gen Z kids planning a colour revolution using this accident?" reads one widely shared post. "Are they trying to emulate Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, and then create an Asian Spring? Remember, this is Vietnam! This is not Nepal, India, or Bangladesh!"

title: My annual performance review made me realize we need to kill performance reviews
description: You hate annual reviews. Your boss hates annual reviews. HR experts hate annual reviews. It's time to finally kill off annual reviews.
fullText:
Is that a bear chasing you, or is it time for your annual performance review? Your body might not be able to tell the difference — both trigger a fight-or-flight response.

While not as immediately dangerous as an ursine attack, almost everyone lives in fear of their annual performance review. A recent Gallup survey found that only two out of 10 employees say their employer manages their performance in a way that actually motivates them to do good work. Even the people running the show know it's a sham: 2% of Fortune 500 chief human resources officers believe their performance management systems inspire improvement.

So why, exactly, do we insist on the once-a-year rigmarole?

The underlying idea is sound. Feedback is important in the workplace. Nobody wants employees guessing willy-nilly how to do their jobs. But annual performance reviews are an imperfect vehicle. They dredge up events far in the rearview mirror or leave out key areas of growth. They produce anxiety for workers, and even a glowing write-up often leads to a minuscule raise, if any. They create busywork for middle managers. We know what works better — frequent, regular, human attention — but companies continue to rely on them because they're the path of least resistance.

"Nobody's held accountable for anything about their performance appraisals except just doing them," says Peter Cappelli, a professor of management at The Wharton School.

We bundle judgment, coaching, compensation, promotion, and development into one dreaded ritual that doesn't sufficiently accomplish any of those goals.

Performance reviews weren't born in the working world — they originated in the military during World War I, where they were used to help determine promotions. The practice migrated into the corporate realm as major companies grew and people began to stay in one place for a lifetime. Various trends in annual reviews have come and gone — sometimes, they've been more punitive, other times, more development-focused. This fungibility helps explain why they've persisted for so long — and why no one's in agreement about what they're meant to accomplish.

In the 1980s, they took a harsher turn, and the idea of improvement faded as more ruthless business practices took hold. Jack Welch at General Electric famously used a "rank and yank" system, where those in the bottom 10% were shown the door. In the 2000s, reviews morphed into more of an incentive exercise, offering employees a promotion- or raise-shaped carrot at the end of the year. In the 2010s, some companies finally started to look around and wonder what the point of all of this was. Big-name firms such as Microsoft, Deloitte, and Adobe said goodbye to their harsher, more rigid schemes and hello to continuous feedback models. An estimated one-third of US companies abandoned traditional reviews by the middle of the decade.

title: Alaska Republicans scramble to educate voters on suspected Dem plant as 'ballot fatigue' threatens race
description: Dan Sullivan faces voter confusion from a candidate look-alike sharing his name as Alaska's ranked choice voting system adds complexity to the Senate race.
fullText:
In addition to fending off a Democratic challenger, Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, is wrestling against confusion caused by a candidate who shares his name — Dan J. Sullivan Jr., an independent — and a shrinking window to clear it up.

Alaska state Sen. James Kaufman, a Republican, said he personally remains worried about conflation between the two.

"I've had at least one person say they had to slow down to make sure they didn't make a mistake. And I can only imagine people who are less engaged in politics — I think it can be confusing," Kaufman said.

Results on Tuesday seem to confirm his hunch.

Sullivan Jr.'s campaign, which has focused on his background as a logger, has meaningfully splintered support from the incumbent Republican candidate in the primary — but not enough to create ambiguity about who the frontrunner was in the primary. Now, the question becomes whether the Sullivan look-alike will have a proportional impact in November, given Alaska's ranked choice voting system, a larger pool of voters and more time for Republicans to warn voters about the dueling Sullivans.

Morning Glory: Alaska's 'Real' Senator Dan Sullivan Stood Up Over Challenger

Former Congresswoman Mary Peltola convincingly led the field on Tuesday, beating out Sen. Sullivan by a 5.4% lead.

Notably, the votes that went to Sullivan Jr. wouldn't have closed the gap entirely had they been cast for the senator, having received just 2.3%.

Even so, Randy Ruedrich, Republican Party chairman from 2000-2013, believes the confusion is evident.

As a state resident, he pointed out that Alaska's lone congressman, Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, had received as much support in his own primary as the top non-Democrats vying for the Senate seat: Sen. Sullivan, Sullivan Jr. and Gerald Heikes, a veteran.

"Nick Begich, without all this entertainment, has 60,061 votes. Nick Begich has slightly less Republican votes than these three Republicans together," Ruedrich said.

"There is some obvious crossover."

Ruedrich noted that Alaska has grappled with voter name confusion before. He recalled that, in 2022, little-known Buzz Kelly advanced to a general election when enough voters confused him with Republican Senate candidate Kelly Tshibaka. Tshibaka had been campaigning using just her first name, effectively creating two "Kelly" candidates.

"We had a lady running who was using her first name to identify herself because her last name is a nightmare," Ruedrich recalled. "We've had identity issues and confusion in the past."

Ruedrich believes that attempts to muddy the waters also go beyond just Sullivan Jr.'s campaign. He pointed out that this year looks different for Heikes — the Republican with the third-most support on Tuesday and a familiar face in Alaska politics.

"Now, why am I bringing up Heikes? He is a perennial candidate. He has run a number of times, but he's always been unfunded," Ruedrich said.

Judge Rules Republican With Same Name As Sen Dan Sullivan Can Stay On Alaska Primary Ballot

"This year, he has a significant contribution of hundreds of thousands of dollars from a Massachusetts liberal who is contributing to this ultra-conservative Republican, and they're running ads saying that Dan Sullivan is not pro-life; he's pro-abortion."

Heikes has backing from groups like Right for Alaska, which has put roughly $1.2 million up to oppose Sen. Sullivan and $410,000 to support Heikes.

It remains unclear if Heikes will advance to the general election as election results are not final.

One notable difference between Alaska's top-four jungle primary and its general election is the implementation of ranked-choice voting in November.

Under this system, voters rank their preferred candidates. If their top choice is eliminated, their support passes on to their next-ranked option. While supporters of the process argue it expands voters' power and greatly increases the influence of candidates that may not otherwise be a top choice, critics believe it also introduces confusion.

Kaufman fears that some voters won't bother to fill out both the "Sullivans" on the ballot to cover their bases.

He believes there are still some voters in Alaska, especially Republicans, who refuse to use the system, citing disagreements with its implementation.

"Some people have a pretty strong traditionalist perspective: one person, one man, one vote," Kaufman said.

"And so, the ballot fatigue where people just don't rank because maybe they disagree with it; there's a pretty strong segment of the population here that just patently disagrees with the rank-choice voting system we ended up with. And they don't necessarily believe in utilizing it."

Both Kaufman and Ruedrich remain unclear about how much confusion the Sullivan Jr. campaign will add in November, but noted that Republicans will likely make it a focus to highlight the issue in the remaining months of the campaign.

Same-name Candidate Disqualified From Key Senate Race Over Alleged Dem Scheme To Confuse Voters

"It has had some blog coverage and some social media coverage," Ruedrich said.

"I expect that's going to go up significantly to get more people to understand what the problem really is," he added.

In terms of proportionality, Sullivan Jr.'s most notable support came from his hometown, Petersburg Kupreanof. There, he received 66 votes to Sen. Sullivan's 213 votes — roughly 33% of the incumbent's support.

Sullivan Jr.'s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Russia is suffering from a slow-motion bank run as the Kremlin scavenges for war funding—and it may start seizing recruits for the military too
description: The financial sector's loss of deposits has created a liquidity crunch so severe that it's threatening Russia's ability to fund its war.
fullText:
A financial crisis that has long been predicted by Russia experts and Kremlin insiders appears to have finally arrived as banks see depositors scramble to pull out their money amid fears it may be seized.

In the first half of August, Russians withdrew $3.4 billion (286.4 billion rubles), according to central bank data cited by the Washington Post. That's after $7.3 billion was withdrawn in July and $4.5 billion in June.

How severe is Russia's current budget deficit crisis?

How does the financial crisis relate to military mobilization?

What's driving Russians to withdraw billions from banks?

What assets might the Russian government seize for funding?

"Drones are flying. Things are burning down. Nervousness is growing. And people's everyday wisdom may be kicking in that they need to have cash under their pillow and not somewhere in banks where it may never be returned," a former finance official told the Post, adding that banks have much of their capital tied in loans elsewhere.

The situation echoes the iconic scene from the movie It's a Wonderful Life, when panicked depositors show up at the Bailey Bros. Building & Loan demanding their cash, only to learn that it's not all there.

The bank run in Russia may not be as dramatic or precipitous. But the stampede out of lenders this year is on track to nearly double the $24.7 billion pace that was seen in 2022, when Vladimir Putin launched his invasion of Ukraine.

Back then, Russia was flush with cash and expected to pay for a short war. But more than four years later, the invasion has turned into a quagmire that has crushed the Kremlin's finances.

The budget is sinking into deeper deficits, the sovereign wealth fund has been nearly depleted, and tax hikes are straining consumers who are already struggling with high inflation.

Moscow has directed banks to offer capital to the defense industry, but many of those loans turned into bad debts. Now, the financial sector's loss of deposits has created a liquidity crunch so severe that it's threatening Russia's ability to fund its war.

Taras Skvortsov, a senior executive at top retail lender Sberbank, told Russian radio that many banks don't have cash on hand to buy government bonds.

In fact, the finance ministry halted bond auctions indefinitely last month amid higher borrowing costs and weak investor demand. The auctions are the Kremlin's main source of domestic borrowing to fill its budget deficit, which hit $76 billion at the end of July.

As the government's sources of funding dry up, ordinary Russians fear their money may be next. The leader of Russia's Communist Party told parliament recently that 130 trillion rubles held in bank accounts should be "mobilized" to address the country's economic and budget woes.

title: Liberia once offered Black Americans a new home. Decades on, it is receiving migrants the US wants out
description: Is Liberia an American dumping ground — or a place where a new generation of arrivals can build a new life?
fullText:
Is Liberia an American dumping ground — or a place where a new generation of arrivals can build a new life?

That's the question Liberians are asking themselves after the first people to be deported to the West African country from the United States arrived in the capital, Monrovia.

The 20 people on the flight from Louisiana were the first to be sent under an agreement that could see up to 1,200 people transferred to Liberia, a country of less than 6 million people, many of them descendants of formerly enslaved Black Americans.

Liberian officials said the new arrivals were from "African and western hemisphere countries."

Liberia is one of several countries that have agreed to take migrants being deported from the US under the Trump administration's anti-immigration crackdown. The arrivals are coming to a nation whose history is deeply tied to migration from the US.

Nearly two centuries ago, free and formerly enslaved Black Americans crossed the Atlantic to settle in what would become Liberia – a name that translates as "land of the free."

Now, a country shaped in part by that migration is accepting people the US wants to remove.

For Liberians, that has thrown up a mix of feelings in a country still recovering from a long and bloody civil war.

"This country is going through a lot, and having more people come in — can we handle all of this?" said Pheta Morris, 48, a descendant of the Black Americans who settled in Liberia.

But she said she sees the new arrivals through the lens of Liberia's history and is struck by the contrast.

"I think about the Americo-Liberians — people who were rejected where they were and needed somewhere to go, and Liberia opened its arms to them," she said.

"Back then, people needed somewhere they could be free, accepted and welcomed. Now, people are being rejected from the US, and Liberia is opening its doors to them."

The first transfer has already faced complications.

A US State Department spokesperson said implementing the Trump administration's immigration policies was a "top priority," adding that the department generally does not comment on private diplomatic communications with other governments.

CNN has contacted Liberia's information ministry 

The first group of free Black Americans arrived in Liberia in the early 1820s.

Over the following decades, thousands more made the journey, with the American Colonization Society helping to establish settlements along the West African coast. The US State Department says about 16,000 Black Americans migrated to Liberia during the 19th century.

The migration was complicated. Some Black Americans saw Liberia as a chance to escape racism and build a new life, while others opposed the colonization movement and rejected the idea that free Black people should leave the US.

Africans rescued from slave ships by the US Navy were also brought to Liberia. The settlements eventually formed the Republic of Liberia, which declared independence in 1847.

The American influence remains visible today. Liberia's flag resembles that of the US; its capital was named Monrovia after America's fifth President James Monroe, and its early institutions were heavily influenced by Washington.

Conmany Wesseh, a former Liberian lawmaker and member of the ruling Unity Party who was nominated as Liberia's ambassador to the United Nations and later the European Union under former president Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, said that history continues to shape how Liberians view the US.

For Wesseh though, the arrival of the deportees raises a more immediate question: Can Liberia, a country still struggling with basic infrastructure and services, accommodate more people?

Liberia began rebuilding after a 14-year civil war ended in 2003, but Wesseh said the country still needs major investment. Poverty levels remain high and youth unemployment stands at 40%, according to African Development Bank data.

"Our country needs a great deal of support," he said. "We are short on medical facilities, and we have problems with education."

He questioned how the country would manage an influx of people from abroad.

"They will have to go to the same hospitals. You won't create a new hospital for them," he said. "There's no spare housing. We don't have existing housing to put new people in."

Wesseh said Liberia's development needs may have influenced the government's decision, with officials hoping the agreement would bring support from Washington.

Liberian authorities described the arrangement as humanitarian and said the deportees will be treated as guests who can seek asylum or leave the country.

Asked whether he viewed the deal as humanitarian assistance, a diplomatic arrangement or the US outsourcing its immigration enforcement, Wesseh chose the latter.

"I think (the administration of US President Donald Trump) just sees this as a place to dump people," he said. "They want to take them off their hands and dump them in this country."

Francis Dennis had long known that his family had roots in the migration of Black Americans to Liberia in the 19th century. But just a few weeks ago, he became curious about his family's past and began using AI genealogy tools to dig deeper into that history.

The 71-year-old former president of the Liberia Chamber of Commerce told CNN he traced his great-great-great-grandfather to Snow Hill, a town on Maryland's Eastern Shore in the US, using the technology and notes left by his father.

He said the research also pointed him to the name of the vessel that carried his ancestor across the Atlantic to Liberia, along with a list of its passengers.

Generations later, Dennis is watching another group arrive in Liberia from the US. But he does not believe their circumstances have to define what comes next.

"People may have their apprehension about a new life, but it's also an opportunity," he said. "Some may be happy, some may resent it, but it opens a new window, a new opportunity."

His own ancestor crossed the Atlantic generations ago and became part of the community that helped shape modern Liberia.

Now, he hopes those arriving under very different circumstances will also see the country as a chance for a fresh start.

"The ball will be in their court," Dennis said. "Are they going to seize it as an opportunity for a new start, a fresh start, a new life? Or will they be thinking about the past?"

title: London Zoo animals hop on scales for weigh-in
description: Kiwi the Capybara is among animals getting their annual health check while data is gathered and shared.
fullText:
Animals at London Zoo are being checked and measured as part of its annual weigh-in day to monitor their health and wellbeing.

Zookeepers will need to coax every bird, reptile, fish and mammal - from the largest rodents in the world to the greenest katydids - to the weighing scale.

Each measurement is added to the Zoological Information Management System (ZIMS), a global database shared with animal carers and conservationists that compares important information on thousands of endangered species.

Many of the zoo's animals are trained to perch on a scale while zookeepers note down their measurements, but others will need to be tempted with a strategic snack.

Although the zoo houses more than 14,000 animals, the keepers will only have time to measure and log the weight of about 400 creatures.

Daniel Simmonds, London Zoo's animal operations manager, said: "Regular weigh-ins help zookeepers track the health of our animals, including invertebrates like the magnolia land snails, the capybaras and Humboldt penguins, and genuinely help us manage the care of these animals, who play a vital role in our global conservation efforts."

Among the animals weighed this year were capybara siblings Kiwi and Gizmo.

Kiwi weighed in at 45kg (7st), while her brother Gizmo tipped the scales at 50.5kg (8st).

While Giant Magnolia Land Snail No 2 weighed a modest 102.5g (3.6oz).

title: China's netizens rage against professor who said gig work was a type of 'welfare'
description: HONG KONG, Aug 24 (Reuters) - The term "flexible employment" has gone viral in China after a prominent economics professor described gig work as a form of "welfare", drawing widespread public anger
fullText:
HONG KONG, Aug 24 (Reuters) - The term "flexible employment" has gone viral in China after a prominent economics professor described gig work as a form of "welfare", drawing widespread public anger and highlighting deep ‌anxieties over job insecurity.

Zhang Dandan, a professor of economics and deputy dean at Peking University's National School ‌of Development, made the remarks during a discussion on social protection for gig workers, on the popular financial show "Let's Talk" last week.

She argued ​that from the perspective of labour economics, "flexibility itself is a form of welfare."

While regular employees trade schedule flexibility for pensions and other benefits, flexible workers enjoy greater control over their time at the cost of weaker social protections, Zhang said.

The comments triggered a fierce backlash over the weekend, with social media users accusing Zhang of being oblivious to the harsh ‌realities of the gig economy.

Zhang did ⁠not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

The controversy has struck a nerve for many in China, where a cooling economy has made secure, full-time employment harder to find.

The China ⁠New Employment Forms Research Center, a think tank, estimates the number of flexible workers — those without permanent full-time contracts — will rise to 320 million this year from 280 million in 2025.

That represents about 44% of China's urban workforce and is roughly ​equivalent to ​the entire population of the United States.

The ​rise of gig jobs in China, where employers ‌are not mandated to make social insurance contributions, heightens long-term risks for China's already strained welfare and pension systems, some industry experts have warned.

Prominent nationalist commentator Hu Xijin, a former editor at the state-backed Global Times newspaper, called Zhang's remarks "shocking" and "unacceptable."

"She has paid the price for her reputation for speaking this way, and the responsibility lies with her," Hu wrote on his Weibo account, adding that she should "respond to public opinion, explain where necessary, and apologize ‌where appropriate."

Despite the backlash, some social media users pointed out Zhang's ​academic career had focused largely on documenting the struggles of gig ​workers and advocating for their social security.

Zhang noted ​last year that on-demand workers made up about 31% of the workforce in China's manufacturing ‌sector.

During peak seasons, that proportion can rise to ​as high as 80% for ​large manufacturers with more than 10,000 workers, she said.

Nevertheless, Zhang's framing of "flexibility" as a benefit was seen as insensitive.

"Such comments from experts are no less than rubbing salt into the wounds of those without job ​security," one Weibo user wrote.

Another user ‌pointed out the relentless pressure faced by delivery drivers and couriers: "Every day, they are racing against the ​platform's algorithm at all costs, without rest... [flexible work] is precisely the most unavoidable of choices, ​not a preference."

title: 8-year-old dies from rare brain-eating amoeba likely contracted while swimming in Louisiana lake
description: An 8-year-old has died after contracting a rare brain-eating amoeba believed to have been encountered while swimming in a lake near her home, her family and health officials said.
fullText:
An 8-year-old has died after contracting a rare brain-eating amoeba believed to have been encountered while swimming in a lake near her home, her family and health officials said.

Lillian Smart, who lived in Ruston in northern Louisiana, died in the hospital over the weekend, shortly after turning 8, according to her parents.

"Last night Lillian ran from our arms to the arms of Jesus," her family said in a post on Facebook Sunday morning. "The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from," the post read.

The family earlier wrote Lillian had experienced significant brain swelling "as a result of the parasite."

The Louisiana Department of Health announced last week a resident had likely contracted the organism, known as Naegleria fowleri, while swimming in Lake Claiborne which is about 30 miles northwest of Ruston.

The microscopic amoeba thrives in warm freshwater and can cause a neurological infection when water containing the amoeba rushes through the nose and reaches the brain, according to the state health department. It can't cause infection if swallowed and does not spread from person to person.

"The infection is extremely rare, but nearly always fatal," the department said.

Health officials did not name Lillian as the infected resident, but friends and family identified her to several local news outlets.

Naegleria fowleri infections are extremely rare, with only 180 confirmed between 1937 and 2025, according to the Louisiana Department of Health. The state has only seen three cases during that period, the department said.

While most cases have been concentrated in southern and central states due the warmer weather, recent research suggests climate change is warming water in northern and midwestern states, expanding the areas where the amoeba can be found.

Early symptoms of contracting the amoeba can include headache, fever, nausea, and vomiting, according to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention. The infection can be hard to detect and progresses rapidly, leading to stiff neck, confusion, hallucinations and loss of balance, it said.

Lillian had been in intensive care since last week after being admitted for a fever that progressed into double vision, according to a post on her mother's Facebook.

Before her death, several Ruston businesses participated in a fundraiser to celebrate Lillian's birthday and donate part of their proceeds to the family, according to CNN affiliate KNOE. Residents said Smart was well known in the community for her joy.

"She's just always a happy child," one local business owner told KNOE. "Every time you see her, she has a smile on her face."

"Everyone did everything they could to keep her here," Lillian's parents said on Facebook. "We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next."

In 2023, a Georgia resident died after contracting the amoeba, and a child in 2022 was Nebraska's first reported death linked to the amoeba, CNN previously reported.

In both cases, health officials said the patients became infected after swimming in fresh water.

title: ‘A sucker born every minute’: The man who duped tourists with a fake Greek amphitheater
description: The Anfiteatro del Berico, a supposed Greek theater in Arcugnano, Italy, had a $46 entry fee. But it was made of concrete and polystyrene.
fullText:
Of the eight TripAdvisor reviews of the amphitheater near Arcugnano, in Italy's northern Veneto region, all give fulsome, five-star praise.

"An enchanting place," reads one review.

"A world beyond space and time," enthuses another. "Definitely one of the best places I have ever been to," raves another.

"Unique on the planet," writes another visitor. That last one was prescient, because the theater certainly was unique. It wasn't Greek, as it purported to be. It wasn't even Roman.

Instead, the "kind custodian" who was "more or less a historian, and an excellent narrator," as one other visitor dubbed him, had built it himself. This month, after a 10-year legal battle, the owner has been jailed for forging works of art, carrying out building works without authorization, and destroying a protected landscape.

The case has scandalized Italy, a country that just edges out China for the most UNESCO World Heritage sites and is home to many legitimate Greek and Roman theaters, from those of Syracuse and Pompeii, where productions are still staged each summer, to the amphitheater of Verona, 40 miles west of Arcugnano, which becomes a mega-stage for opera each summer.

Franco Malosso, the owner, creator and self-styled discoverer of the nearly 54,000-square-foot "ancient" site, charged visitors up to 40 euros ($46) to visit the "theater" he had built from scratch.

On a scenic hillside, employing a local construction firm, he had built seating and steps, which, according to evidence presented in court, he had artificially aged, then added a smattering of cement columns and plaster statues over the small "lake" that he had dug out himself.

The traditional tiered seating, which he said had been built by hand by the ancient Greeks over 2,000 years ago, was constructed by 21st-century builders using machines. They used newly quarried stone from Puglia and cement, while a supporting wall was topped with polystyrene, according to court documents shared with CNN.

"Just the idea of it is insane," Darius Arya, archaeologist and director of Ancient Rome Live, told CNN, calling Malosso's scheme "diabolical" and "terrible."

Malosso, according to evidence presented in court, is said to have hosted concerts and performances inside the site, which went by no fewer than three names: Anfiteatro Berico, Anfiteatro Marittimo Berico and Anfiteatro Porta degli Angeli. He also led guided visits around the site, according to prosecutors.

For anyone with a basic knowledge of ancient history, there were red flags aplenty. Malosso's building was a fan-shaped theater, not an amphitheater, which is oval. It wasn't near the sea, as "Marittimo" implies — Arcugnano is around 50 miles from the coast. There wasn't an ancient "Angels' Gate" (Porta degli Angeli) at the site, either. Nor could it have been Greek — while northern Italy is replete with Roman remains, the ancient Greeks only colonized farther south.

Not that the visitors, who raved about the concrete columns and chalk statues, seemed to have cared.

Nor did they seem to notice that where there should have been a stage, Malosso — who also went by the name of Von Rosenfranz — had excavated a photogenic pool of water.

"Why was there a pool of water there, there were no maritime performances," said Arya. "It's like a folly — it doesn't feel right."

The dupe theater, on a hillside covered in protected woodland outside the small town of Arcugnano, just over three miles south of Vicenza, was discovered by local law enforcement, who immediately referred it to the cultural superintendency in October 2016.

A site inspection was carried out by a representative of the local heritage board and police from the Carabinieri's Nucleo Tutela Patrimonio Artistico (TPC), the division known in English as the "art squad" for its work investigating stolen artworks and forgeries.

The theater was so clearly fake that the inspection was concluded in a single day, Lt. Col. Giuseppe Marseglia, commander of the TPC in Monza, which covers northern Italy, told CNN. Marseglia called it a "truly obscene" attempt at forgery. "Of all criminals, forgers are the ones with the most talent, because they are able to create works of art," he said. "Then there are scammers … I have no respect [for Malosso]. Calling him a forger is an offense to forgers."

Marseglia said that in his 25 years in the force, he had never seen or heard of an entire archaeological site being faked.

The theater was constructed on land that was part of the UNESCO-protected Berici Hills landscape. Malosso — who claimed to be the legal representative of the land owner, a business based in the British Virgin Islands — had originally applied for planning permission to build a garage, according to court documents. Instead, he hired local builders to construct the theater, instructing them to "make it look old," according to one of them, who gave evidence in court.

Prosecutors said he told visitors that he had discovered it after a landslide and advertised it to the public starting in 2014, including writing to the mayor of Arcugnano to explain how profitable the site could be. Ticket-holders were told that the site had been visited by Julius Caesar, Cleopatra, and Juliet Capulet, the fictional character invented by William Shakespeare.

Unearthing the theater like Malosso claimed wouldn't be reasonably possible, says Mauro Puddo, an archeologist specializing in the Roman world and researcher at the Università per Stranieri di Siena. According to Puddu, at the standard rate of excavation only a maximum of one row of seats per year could be revealed as part of an extensively planned and carefully monitored excavation.

"You're not allowed to dig up antiquities in your backyard," Arya added. "You have to declare it, they investigate it, they excavate. This is terrible."

Visitors from out of town were charged 12 euros ($14), according to local media, while locals were disincentivized with a 40 euro ($46) charge. Private group tours were also reportedly available at a cost of 600 euros ($692) for 45 minutes. Marseglia said the charges were framed as a "minimum contribution for the upkeep of the site." It is not known how many victims took the bait but the site was only reported to the authorities in 2016, two years after its opening.

"I guess there's a sucker born every minute, but I suppose when you have something advertised, people think this is the real deal," said Arya.

Malosso was convicted in 2019 and lost an initial appeal in 2020. He made a final appeal to the Corte di Cassazione, Italy's supreme court, arguing — among other things — that his forgery was so obvious that nobody could have reasonably believed it to be true.

The Cassazione rejected his arguments and reaffirmed the original sentence, which he is now serving, including a 28-month jail term and a fine of 3,000 euros ($3,462) plus 3,500 euros ($4,040) in legal fees. Since his original conviction, the law has been tightened to allow sentences of up to five years for forgery, said Marseglia.

Why Malosso embarked on his scheme is a mystery, experts told CNN. For starters, he apparently hadn't done his homework. The ancient Greeks never colonized anywhere as far north as Vicenza, said Marseglia, who called it "crazy."

Arya was baffled at what the plan was. "You can tell it's fake immediately," he said.

One photo from the site's Facebook page shows a visibly cement column accompanied by a rather modern-looking sculpture of a man, which turned out to be made from plaster.

"The columns are clearly modern," said Peter Matthaes, director of Milan's Museo di Arte e Scienza, which is partly dedicated to the art of forgery.

Matthaes said that he thought perhaps Malosso's skills as a raconteur could have swept visitors along. "From a few comments on the internet you realize that the visitors were accompanied by a narrator to turn the visit into an experience. How many times are we in front of this situation? How many times are we told a story — by advertisements, in politics or in the media trying to convince us of what is the 'truth,' when in reality the truth is something different?"

Malosso's theater-amphitheater is hardly the first fake to hit the headlines, says Puddu, who points to the Renaissance-era Donation of Constantine — a forged Roman imperial decree that transferred imperial authority to the Pope — as the most famous fake of classical history.

Rome's Museo di Arte Salvata, or Museum of Rescued Art, exhibits both stolen and forged works of ancient art in an ancient Roman bathhouse, while Matthaes' Museo di Arte e Scienza devotes an entire floor to archaeological and artistic forgery.

Marseglia said that forgery of antiquities started in the Renaissance. Today, he said, a 15th-century forgery of a Roman medal would be more valuable than an actual Roman artifact.

"It's a very vast topic," said Puddu. "I understand why archaeologists are horrified, but I understand why you might feel a grudging respect."

"Forgeries are a part of human civilization — we try to trick each other all the time," he said. "A foundational text of humanity, the 'Odyssey' and also the 'Iliad' are based on a trick — an illusion, a forgery."

The site has now been sequestered and Malosso was ordered to tear down the theater, though its fate remains to be seen. Arya warned that it will be an expensive job.

"I'd hate to think of seeing taxpayer money going to remove something like that," he said. The mayor of Arcugnano recently told La Repubblica that he would not spend public money on it. He did not respond to a request for an interview from CNN. Nor did the attorney who represented Malosso in his supreme court appeal. His attorney from his original trial declined to comment.

As for those interested in seeing legitimate sites, Arya recommends Verona for an amphitheater, or Aquileia, two and a half hours northeast on Veneto's border with Friuli. The Roman city is accompanied by a church with early Christian mosaics.

The area around Arcugnano is rich in history, says Andrea Rosignoli, the superintendent for the Ministry of Culture for Vicenza. Within Arcugnano's territory is the Lago di Fimon, which was once home to Neolithic stilted structures on the lakeside. The Berici Hills are home to various prehistoric caves, he said, recommending the Grotta di San Bernardino, while genuine Roman sites are on lower ground nearby. Rosignoli also recommended the Museo Civico Naturalistico-Archeologico in Vicenza, which has finds from Lake Fimon and Teatro Berga, an actual Roman theater that once stood in the city center.

Meanwhile, for Puddu, two of the best-preserved Roman theaters are at Amman in Jordan and Orange, France. Closer to home, he recommends the one in Lecce, Puglia, which sits in the main square.

In the meantime, in Arcugnano, the entrance to Malosso's theater is still visible. A modern-looking stone wall and huge metal gate are accompanied by signs detailing the supposed history of the site. One mentions that the house where Juliet Capulet grew up is within the complex, including a balcony, with no reference to her being a fictional Shakespearean character. Another mentions an ancient burial site.

Locals say that the theater used to be visible from the road below, but today it is covered entirely by thick undergrowth. If the plans to destroy the theater are followed through, the process will, ironically, have to start with an excavation. Only this time, a real one.

title: Scott's world title aim after testing personal period
description: Olympic champion Hannah Scott is preparing for the World Championships in Amsterdam which begin on Tuesday after her "most successful winter of training so far".
fullText:
Olympic champion Hannah Scott says she will arrive at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam on the back of her "most successful winter of training so far".

The Coleraine sculler says her experience to date in the sport is becoming "more and more useful, which is even showing across the team".

Scott won Olympic gold in Paris two years ago but her story has been a rollercoaster ride of injury and illness as well as success and joy.

On the water, life is good, and the public will get to see that this week as Scott and her team-mates compete in the Netherlands.

But, away from competition, elite athletes like Scott face the same challenges as anyone else and she has opened up about some of the issues she has had to navigate.

"In my personal life, I've had my hiccups and ups and downs. My life was turned upside down at Christmas time, when I went through a serious breakup and I've had to manage that," said Scott.

"But in terms of my life in the boat and training, I've managed to keep that all going this year and it shows in terms of my performances.

"That was the one thing I was really stubborn about. I wasn't going to let anything happening in my personal life impact my rowing and my career which I've put so much work towards."

Compartmentalising life and not bringing personal problems to training that could affect performance and other athletes around them is part and parcel of life as an athlete.

It is something Scott has learned to do, especially during that difficult spell last year which coincided with an important period of training.

"When I talk about what happened at Christmas time, it all happened during a really testing period in rowing. We were going through a lot of trials which ended up dictating a bit of our selection for the year," she added.

"I actually didn't share a lot of what was going on at Christmas time, because I knew everyone in the boat would probably then be worried about what was happening.

"You tell your friends, you get the support where you need it, but in terms of when you're in training, and for me, working in such a high-pressure environment, that type of thing can actually distract quite a lot.

"It's easier to try and find your support systems where you can with your family and your friends, and then keep your performance separate, because when you bring too much emotion into it, even happy emotion, I do think it can sometimes distract you from what you're trying to do.

"It's a skill I've had to learn a lot 

Scott is now setting her sights on winning a second world title in the women's quad sculls alongside fellow Northern Ireland rower Finnola Stratton as well as Imogen Grant and Lola Anderson.

In Amsterdam they will face world champions the Netherlands on home water, but Switzerland and Germany will also provide stiff opposition.

There is also a new quad from Ireland that includes 19-year-old Sophia Young from Belfast, who recently took silver in the single sculls at the world under-23 championships.

"The event itself is starting to stack up, and that's where I'm excited to see where we land on it, because, with everyone else that's improving, I think we've seen a massive breakthrough, is how I would describe it, in the past five weeks and what we've done in our crew," added Scott.

"I want to see where that lands and how that lands and hopefully we can display that in what's going to be an amazing event at this World Championships."

title: Rising star Yamashita ties LPGA scoring record
description: Rising star Miyu Yamashita ties an LPGA Tour scoring record as she surges to a dominant nine-shot victory at the CPKC Women's Open in Canada.
fullText:

Rising star Miyu Yamashita tied an LPGA Tour scoring record as she surged to a dominant nine-shot victory at the CPKC Women's Open in Canada.

The 25-year-old from Japan made an eight-foot birdie putt on the 18th hole to complete a four-under 66 on Sunday and finish the week on a 23-under 257.

It matched Kim Sei-young 72-hole tour record lowest total, with the South Korean also carding 257 when finishing 31 under at Thornberry Creek in 2018.

Yamashita broke the tournament's record of 262, set by South Korea's Ko Jin-young in 2019.

Having dominated from the opening round, Yamashita headed into the final day with a six-shot lead and extended that with six birdies in a closing four-under 66 on the Royal Mayfair course.

Her compatriot Yuri Yoshida finished a distant second at 14 under par, while Kim Sei-young was another shot back in third.

It is a fourth LPGA victory in 13 months for Yamashita, who was named the tour's rookie of the year for 2025 after winning her first major at the Women's Open.

title: Four arrested over murder of two-time world champion Tete
description: One of the suspects is due in court on Monday to be charged with murder and attempted murder.
fullText:
Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday.

Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital.

One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges.

Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014. He was later given a four-year ban, which lapsed in July this year.

The remaining suspects, who were arrested on Sunday, are due in court on Tuesday. Two have been charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition. It is unclear whether they will also be charged with murder and attempted murder.

Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27‑year‑old female passenger, according to officials.

The motive behind the attack is unclear.

Tributes have been pouring in for the two-time world champion since his death. South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced."

Former Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula also paid tribute to Tete, lamenting the loss of a "a great South African who has made an immense contribution in the sport of boxing".

Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom.

He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017.

Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test.

He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency.

After his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight after his ban ended.

Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest.

South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world.

According to the latest crime statistics, covering the period between January and March this year, around 58 people were killed each day.

title: Maradona's 'Hand of God' ball sells for £2.5m
description: The football with which Diego Maradona scored his famous 'hand of God' goal in the 1986 World Cup quarter-final victory over England is sold at auction.
fullText:
The football with which Diego Maradona scored his famous 'hand of God' goal at the 1986 World Cup has sold at auction for £2.5m.

Maradona famously punched the ball past goalkeeper Peter Shilton in Argentina's 2-1 quarter-final win over England.

After the game, he told reporters it had been scored "a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God".

Maradona later scored what became known as the 'goal of the century' in the same game, dribbling past five England outfield players before slotting the ball past Shilton.

Though it sold for $3.3m (£2.5m) at Heritage Auctions in the United States on Saturday, the ball had been expected to fetch nearer $10m (£7.3m).

Speaking to Reuters before the auction, Mike Provenzale, a specialist auctioneer at Heritage, said: "It's a true one-of-one item. Arguably the most significant soccer item that exists."

Tunisian Ali Bin Nasser, who refereed the match in 1986, collected the Adidas Azteca ball at full-time and kept it for more than three decades.

In 2023, he signed a letter to confirm it was the only ball used during the match, which has also been confirmed by further independent authentication.

Bin Nasser sold the ball in 2022 for $2.37m (£1.74m). Its new owner again put it up for auction in 2023 though it did not sell as bids did not meet the minimum value set.

The shirt worn by Maradona during the same match sold for £7.1m at auction in 2022.

title: One in 322 billion - club golfer defies birdie odds
description: Amateur golfer Allan Harrison - a former foursomes partner of Tommy Fleetwood - defies astronomical odds to card eight birdies across just nine holes.
fullText:
An ordinary round of golf turned into an extraordinary masterclass as an English amateur defied astronomical odds to card eight birdies across just nine holes.

Allan Harrison started his round at Fairhaven Golf Club with four dropped shots on the front nine before a "pasty and a drink" at the halfway house gave him a burst of life.

The 64-year-old then fired seven consecutive birdies and eight in nine holes - a run of form rarely seen in professional golf, let alone at an amateur level.

Harrison has some prowess as a former foursomes partner of Tommy Fleetwood at Southport and Ainsdale Golf Club.

England Golf calculated the odds across all amateur golfers for making eight birdies in nine holes as an astonishing one in 322 billion.

For Harrison, whose 0.4 handicap signals a high level of ability, the odds were said to be one in 455,000.

The leader in birdie average on the PGA Tour typically records around 4.8-5.0 birdies per 18 holes, which equates to 2.5 per nine holes.

"I was four over after the front nine," Harrison said.

"I went into the halfway house, had a pasty and a drink, and the lads laughed when I said I'd start the back nine fresh."

Had he run up nine consecutive birdies, Harrison would have achieved the same tally as the PGA Tour's record - with nine having been achieved by American Mark Calcavecchia at the 2009 Canadian Open and fellow US player Kevin Chappell at the Greenbrier in 2019.

But he just missed out on a place in the record books despite almost holing his tee-shot at the 157-yard par-three 17th.

"My playing partner pointed out the pitch mark and said I must've nearly holed out - but it ran six feet past and I misread the putt," said Harrison of his only par on the back nine.

Harrison led the Silver Pheasant tournament on 40 points after the first round, but he could not replicate his heroics on the second day as he finished second overall.

Although England Golf's calculations point to an extraordinarily high unlikelihood of an amateur golfer having eight birdies in nine holes, Harrison is not alone in having achieved the feat in 2026.

Only last month, Australian Amelia Harris, 18, had eight in nine on her back nine, external in the first round of the US Girls' Junior tournament in Durham, North Carolina.
