title: Gauff gears up for US Open with Cincinnati triumph
description: Coco Gauff powers past Jessica Pegula in the final of the Cincinnati Open to win her first title of 2026 just before the US Open, as Arthur Fils wins the men's event.
fullText:
Coco Gauff powered past third seed Jessica Pegula in the final of the Cincinnati Open to win her first title of 2026 and make a statement before the US Open.

The 22-year-old American needed only an hour and 14 minutes to defeat compatriot Pegula 6-2 6-4 as she became just the third two-time champion of the WTA 1000 event, joining Serena Williams and Victoria Azarenka.

When Gauff won the Cincinnati trophy in 2023, she went on to win her first Grand Slam title at the the US Open three weeks later.

"I think with each match, I was feeling more and more confident in trusting the work that I put in and the practice - knowing that I can figure out these matches," said world number four Gauff, who dropped just one set in Cincinnati.

"It's going to be tough in New York, but just knowing the quality wins that I had this week, knowing that I'm able to figure it out even if I'm not playing my best, but also knowing that I can play that great tennis that I felt like I was playing this week."

Qualifying for the US Open started on Sunday, while the main draw begins on Sunday, 30 August.

In the men's final, Arthur Fils secured the first ATP Masters 1,000 title of his career by holding off American home hope Frances Tiafoe in a 6-3 1-6 6-0 win.

Fils, 22, has long been one of the best young players on the tour, but his career has been disrupted by a series of injuries.

However, he has now won two ATP Tour titles since returning in February after nine months on the sidelines with a stress fracture in his back.

"Wow, that feels good. That feels good," said Fils, who rises to a career-high 11th in the world rankings.

"It's a lot of training, a lot of things, a lot of sacrifice. Injury. To be able to win one title like this means a lot to me."

title: Boks drop Feinberg-Mngomezulu to bench for All Blacks rematch
description: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu pays for an indifferent showing in South Africa's series opener against New Zealand, as the fly-half drops to the Springbok bench.
fullText:
Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu has paid the price for an indifferent showing in South Africa's defeat by New Zealand, with the fly-half dropping to the bench for Saturday's rematch in Cape Town.

The All Blacks, revitalised under new coach Dave Rennie, ran out 33-16 winners in the series opener in Johannesburg.

Feinberg-Mngomezulu was turned over five times in possession and occasionally exposed in defence, before he shifted to full-back for the Springboks in the second half of Saturday's first Test.

South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has recalled 32-year-old double Rugby World Cup winner Handre Pollard at 10, while injuries to Cheslin Kolbe and Grant Williams have brought Ethan Hooker and Cobus Reinach into the starting line-up at wing and scrum-half respectively.

Siya Kolisi may return to the back row after recovering from a hamstring injury, but Erasmus has also named Paul de Villiers as a back-up at blindside flanker in case Kolisi is not ready.

Thirty-nine year-old Deon Fourie, who came off the bench to play 77 minutes of the Springboks' 2023 Rugby World Cup final win over New Zealand, could win his first cap since that occasion after being named among the replacements.

"There were a handful of positives and negatives last week, but the main thing that let us down was that we created so many chances, but mistakes at crucial times cost us," said Erasmus.

"We'll put in a lot of work this week to ensure that we are sharp in that regard this weekend because if we had used even some of those chances, the result could have been completely different."

South Africa side to face New Zealand: Willemse; Arendse, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Pollard, Reinach; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Nortje, Kolisi/De Villiers, PS du Toit, Wiese.

Replacements: Fourie, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, Esterhuizen, Hanekom, Van den Berg, Feinberg-Mngomezulu.

New Zealand may be tempted to give Richie Mo'unga an immediate Test return as they chase a 2-0 lead in the four-match series that has been marketed as 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry'.

The 32-year-old was first-choice stand-off during their 2023 Rugby World Cup campaign, but he has been ineligible for selection while playing his club rugby in Japan since.

However, his signing for Canterbury and the Crusaders, along with an injury to Billy Proctor, has paved the way for his comeback.

Mo'unga will start at 10 in Tuesday's match against Johannesburg-based provincial side the Lions.

Mo'unga, who says his determination to return to Tests was fuelled by watching a Six Nations match while in a Japanese karaoke bar last year, is confident he can produce the form that earned him a spot in World Rugby's team of 2023.

"I'm competitive; I want to be the best," he said. "I know that there's a process to that, and at this point in time, the process looks a bit different around preparing someone else [All Blacks' current first-choice fly-half Ruben Love] to be the best.

"I'm really competitive, but I'm also a team man. Whoever gets the role, gets the role, and if it's not me, I'll do anything I can to help them succeed.

"This game was always coming for me. There was always going to be a return. I wasn't sure when it was, but mentally I've prepared for my return in the black jersey, and I'm ready."

title: Fans suffer firework burns and eye injuries in Eredivisie
description: Dutch side SC Cambuur says fans were left with "burns, hearing damage and eye injuries"  after Feyenoord supporters threw fireworks during Sunday's Eredivisie match.
fullText:
Dutch club SC Cambuur said fans have suffered "burns, hearing damage and eye injuries" after Feyenoord supporters threw fireworks during Sunday's league match.

Play was suspended for around 10 minutes in the first half after visiting fans in the away end at the Kooi Stadion lit a large number of red flares and threw fireworks.

Some of the fireworks were aimed towards sections containing home fans and SC Cambuur said in a statement that five supporters were confirmed to have been injured.

Feyenoord said it "firmly distances itself from the unacceptable events" and that head coach Giovanni van Bronckhorst - an assistant to Arne Slot at Liverpool last season - apologised on behalf of the club to SC Cambuur after the match.

"It should be clear that setting off and firing fireworks is completely unacceptable and has no place in a football stadium whatsoever," SC Cambuur said.

The club, who were promoted to the Eredivisie last season after three seasons in the Dutch second tier, said it would work with the authorities to make sure those responsible were punished, while Feyenoord said they would request camera footage.

Last season, an Eredivisie match between Ajax and Groningen was abandoned after fireworks and flares were ignited behind one of the goals at Johan Cruyff Arena.

Feyenoord's general manager Robert Eenhoorn said he "cannot be happy" with their 5-2 victory in Leeuwarden, adding "frustration prevails too much for that".

"This problem obviously does not only affect Feyenoord and is unfortunately something we have been unable to put a stop to for decades," Eenhoorn said.

"We will therefore have to sit down again with all stakeholders, clubs, the KNVB [Dutch football association], and the authorities to look for a solution together."

Leeuwarden mayor Foort van Oosten also condemned the incident and promised an investigation, while the Dutch football association said it would revisit its protocols for incidents of disorder.

The game resumed despite the injuries to the fans, but it would have been abandoned had a player or match official been hit.

"That doesn't feel right," Jan Bluyssen, the KNVB's manager of professional football competition affairs, told Dutch news agency ANP.

"We need to examine whether the protocol is still appropriate and how we might want to adjust it."

title: Alonso 'always thinking' but Arbeloa becoming boss 'a surprise' - Benitez
description: Former Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez on his former players Xabi Alonso and Alvaro Arbeloa who face each other as managers on Monday when Fulham host Chelsea.
fullText:
When former Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez is asked whether he had expected his then-players Xabi Alonso and Alvaro Arbeloa to become managers, his response is brutally honest.

"Alonso, yes. Arbeloa, not really," he says. "For me, Arbeloa was a surprise."

Almost 20 years after Benitez brought them together at Anfield, the pair will go head-to-head as Arbeloa's Fulham host Alonso's Chelsea on Monday.

The pair won the 2010 World Cup and two European Championships with Spain, along with domestic league and cup triumphs when they both joined Real Madrid after Liverpool.

They played together for seven years at club level and shared the pitch 262 times for club and country, and their careers have remained closely intertwined since.

Arbeloa was promoted from Real Madrid B to replace Alonso when he was sacked by the Spanish giants in January last season.

"He was in Castilla [Real Madrid's academy], which was similar to how I started, and then he went to Madrid in special circumstances," Benitez said of Arbeloa's rise to Real manager.

They both returned to England in July to take up their first Premier League managerial roles and now lead clubs whose stadiums are only two miles apart.

"With Alvaro, he knows the Premier League," Benitez told BBC Sport. "But his experience is shorter than Xabi's. We need to know how he can cope outside Real Madrid, which protects you in a way. Outside, you are on your own."

It's no surprise that, having played as team-mates – including under Jose Mourinho and Carlo Ancelotti at Real Madrid, and Vicente del Bosque with Spain – socialised off the pitch and even gone on holiday together, the pair are, in the words of Arbeloa, "very good friends", despite being "rivals when the game starts". He explained they spoke to each other in the lead up to Monday's match, but not about football.

Other similarities will see the duo live close to each other in Cobham, Surrey, with their children attending the same school.

In the words of Arbeloa, their friendship "will never change".

Alonso was one of Benitez's first Liverpool signings in 2004 as he looked to overhaul Gerard Houllier's squad, Arbeloa then joining in 2007 from Deportivo after rising through the ranks at Real Madrid.

Benitez explained that Alonso has experience of "coaching at a different level in a different country", having had success in the Bundesliga at Bayer Leverkusen by winning a league and cup double in 2024.

Alonso, in particular, had "vision" on the pitch, says Benitez, while his experiences playing at Liverpool, Real Madrid and then under Pep Guardiola at Bayern Munich would have "opened his mind" to a range of coaching approaches.

Benitez recalls a moment of magic from Alonso in a 2009 game that displayed his football intelligence.

In a match against Sam Allardyce's Blackburn at Anfield, Alonso ignored an instruction to deliver a free-kick to the far post. Instead, his ball to the near post allowed Fernando Torres to head in his second goal of the match as Liverpool went on to win 4-0.

"He was someone who was always thinking," said Benitez.

It is not just Alonso and Arbeloa who are among Benitez's former Liverpool players to have moved into management.

He reels off more than 20 names who have become coaches or managers, a list including Wales boss Craig Bellamy. He also points out that Djimi Traore is now an assistant coach at Seattle Sounders.

"I sent him to the shower at half-time in the Champions League final [in 2005]," he recalled of the defender, who was expecting to be substituted after a poor first-half before an injury to Steve Finnan saw him reinstated for Liverpool's historic second-half comeback and eventual victory on penalties against AC Milan in 2005.

He added: "They always take something from you. Maybe two or three things they can use [as a coach], and I'm happy with that."

It has been more than 40 years since Benitez began coaching at Real Madrid and, this summer, he finds himself in the unusual position of being without a job.

Now 66, Benitez says he is "waiting for another challenge", adding that his passion for the game is undiminished, as is his desire to "improve teams and players".

He felt he delivered in his most recent role at Panathinaikos, securing the top-four finish he had been tasked with achieving when he took the job in October, but was still sacked in May.

Explaining his continued motivation, Benitez said: "I was a PE teacher before and was trying to improve young people. It was the same as when I had Anthony Gordon at Everton."

The former Newcastle and Chelsea manager remains a Uefa technical observer and speaks about adapting to the modern game, using social media, artificial intelligence and increasingly sophisticated data as part of his approach.

"I had some offers," Benitez said, having recently been linked with the Scotland job.

"Maybe it is a national team, as a lot of teams will change after the World Cup, but there has to be something where you feel you can achieve something, whether that is promotion, like we had at Newcastle, with amazing fans.

"I know football now is more demanding. You have to be patient because, if not, if you change with the pressure of social media and change every seven months, then you don't have any project. That is the difficult thing."

title: DeChambeau proud of what LIV has achieved
description: Bryson DeChambeau says he is "proud" of what LIV Golf has achieved with the breakaway league facing questions about its future following the final event of the season in Indianapolis.
fullText:
Bryson DeChambeau says he is "proud" of what LIV Golf has achieved as the breakaway league faces questions about its future following the final event of the season in Indianapolis.

The league, which launched in 2022 as an alternative to the PGA Tour, has faced an uncertain future since Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) withdrew its financial backing in April.

Last week, its season-ending Team Championships in Michigan was cancelled, meaning the event in Indianapolis concluded the 2026 campaign.

LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil has said new investors have been secured for next season but has been tight-lipped on the league's future plans and structure.

American DeChambeau, who led a selection of star players in joining LIV Golf four years ago, said although the breakaway league has not been perfect, it has "a lot of potential moving forward".

"It has been an interesting ride, that's for sure, everything we've gone through, and the tough moments we've had. It's made us stronger," said DeChambeau.

"As much as we are transitioning from LIV 1.0 to LIV 2.0, I have great thoughts about what could happen next year. I wish I could be more upfront about it.

"Ultimately I'm proud of the fact of what we've done, the good and some of the bad that we've unfortunately had, things that have occurred, I'm going to be real with it, not everything was perfect.

"But for the most part we've done a solid job and if there's one thing I could say, we did something different in the game of golf and I'm proud of that."

At the end of the interview, DeChambeau added: "I think there's something fun coming."

Strained smiles and uncertainty - the strange end of LIV Golf 1.0

LIV cancels final event to focus on 'next chapter'

'Tough road back' to PGA Tour from LIV - McIlroy

Last week, Rory McIlroy said it could be a "tough road back" to the PGA Tour for those who leave LIV Golf.

LIV spent £3.7bn, luring players like DeChambeau with lucrative contracts and significant prize money.

Spain's Jon Rahm, who has been crowned the league's individual champion for a third consecutive year, has faced speculation about his future with LIV but says it has not affected his performances.

"There's been a lot that has surrounded all of us pretty much since we joined. At the end of the day, once you step on the golf course it's just golf," said Rahm.

"All the problems and theories go away and you compete. It hasn't been any harder or easier. That is the life of a pro athlete, you deal with things like that."

American rookie Michael La Sasso pipped Rahm to win the event in Indianapolis, carding a final-round 65 to finish on 18-under-par.

Rahm finished one shot behind on 17-under, with DeChambeau and Spain's Sergio Garcia tying for third a further shot back.

La Sasso, 22, executed a perfect chip on the final hole before a tap-in birdie to become the youngest winner of a LIV Golf event.

title: After more than 15 years of laptops in the classroom, do Australian schools need a rethink?
description: ‘We don’t want distraction, we want concentration’: many teachers and parent groups think its time for a ‘digital...
fullText:
‘We don’t want distraction, we want concentration’: many teachers and parent groups think its time for a ‘digital detox’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Earlier this month, the federal education minister, Jason Clare, took to Facebook. “When I was a kid there was a computer room at school. Now they are everywhere. From morning till night,” he wrote. “I think there is a good argument our kids need a digital detox.”

Since that post, as the minister told ABC News Breakfast last week, he has been “inundated” with support from parents and teachers.

Clare’s comments followed the Victorian government’s announcement that it will abolish the use of bring your own device (BYOD) programs in primary schools and limit screen use to 90 minutes per day for years 3 to 6 from January next year. High schools have been instructed to enforce screen-free learning blocks for all students. The then premier Jacinta Allen launched the policy in July, saying: “Less time on devices means more time learning.”

Computer use has expanded rapidly in schools in Australia and worldwide. “Computer rooms” like those in Clare’s days have been replaced by a laptop in most high school students’ backpacks, touted more than 15 years ago as the “toolbox of the 21st century” and essential to equipping students with the skills they would need for the future.

However, the latest Naplan results (described by some commentators in the media as a “national tragedy”) have sparked a re-examination of the long-held concerns of some teachers, parents and experts about the implications of unstructured digital exposure in educational settings. While research linking screen usage to student performance is limited, a change.org petition that calls for a rethink of device reliance in classrooms – and cites the recent Naplan results – has so far garnered more than 25,000 signatures.

This unease has yielded an increasing political appetite to consider changing policy and already prompted a few Australian schools to go back to pen and paper where technology offers no explicit educational benefit.

This reckoning isn’t limited to Australia. Across the world many tech-forward school systems are wrestling with declining academic results and concerns about student wellbeing; the regional government in Madrid earlier this year announced a reduction of tech-time in primary school and Sweden is considering a reduced emphasis on technology in its 2028 curriculum.

The US advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens has successfully campaigned for changes to policy in LAUSD, the country’s second-largest school district: the change will see middle schoolers have just one hour of screen time per week, per subject, and high schoolers limited to 90 minutes per course over the week. Students there will no longer take home school devices unless parents opt-in. In the UK, advocacy group Closed Screens Open Minds, which has garnered celebrity support from the likes of Hugh Grant and Sophie Winkleman, says it’s “building a comprehensive evidence-based resource for parents, teachers, and policymakers to challenge the adoption of EdTech in schools”.

The idea of reducing ambient screen time in class is increasingly popular among parents and teachers, with many complaining of the lack of ability to monitor what a child is doing on a personal laptop as well as fearing for their ability to concentrate, think deeply and learn effectively while using devices connected to the internet.

Jane has been teaching in New South Wales schools for more than 30 years. She says since bringing personal devices into every class became the norm, her students’ “capacity for human interaction is dissolving and their attention spans are shocking”.

Two decades ago, the performing arts and English teacher says students could be shown a video, read a text, or consider some artwork and discuss it for the duration of the lesson.

“Now I have to change up my room and my delivery every 12 minutes to keep them engaged.

“Once upon a time when you studied something, you sat on it, you pondered, you discussed it, and they can’t do that because their world is just flicking, flicking, flicking, flicking … They struggle to think critically or retain any information.

“And there’s not one teacher that I talk to who doesn’t feel the same.”

In response to the Swedish education ministry’s proposal for a national digitisation strategy, the Karolinska Institute – one of the world’s most prestigious medical research institutions – cited studies that show that when university students had their laptops open during lectures they spent up to 40% of the time “on irrelevant things that had no connection to the teaching”. They extrapolated that for younger people, whose executive function is less developed, the effect may be even more significant.

However, while research has shown that writing by hand activates more neural networks than typing, reading from hard copies tends to produce better comprehension over screens and multitasking degrades working memory, confounding factors – such as socio-economic status and subject and teacher-specific implementation – make it incredibly difficult to quantitatively measure the impact of digital device use on students’ learning writ large.

What most experts and educators do seem to agree on is that the crux of the issue is not just screen time, but how and why devices are being used.

The origins of the rapid-scale adoption of devices in Australian schools is the Digital Education Revolution. Launched by the Rudd government in 2008, it aimed to put a laptop in the hands of every Australian high schooler by 2011.

“But we know that schools did not have the necessary structures or support around [the rollout],” says Prof Therese Keane, assistant dean of research and industry engagement at Latrobe University’s faculty of education. Explicit digital instruction was scant, teachers were underqualified and “kids were using them by osmosis”.

“What ultimately happened was they were just using them to replace pen and paper.”

In 2013 the funding dried up. BYOD policies soon proliferated and these days the majority of Australian high school students have their own family-funded device for use throughout the school day.

Keane is a staunch proponent of the benefits technology can bring to education: she believes that 1:1 device access has significant potential, when it’s done right. But between poor classroom management, gaps in the ICT curriculum, nebulous teaching aims related to device usage and “parents’ screen habits at home”, she thinks that the average student is probably labouring through an implementation failure.

An international study from 2022 of the “learning time” of 15-year-old students pointed to a “new type of disciplinary problem – digital distractions”, with one in three students on average across OECD countries reporting that in most or every mathematics lesson, they get distracted using digital devices. Around one in four students indicated that they get distracted by other students who are using digital devices. The same study highlighted that there is a place for digital learning, but that it depends on how devices are used.

Over the past 12 years Laura has worked short-term contacts at 10 schools, across two states, in the Catholic and state systems. She only allows students to open their laptops for specific tasks but, even then, she says, “as soon as those laptops are open, it’s message the mate two rows behind you, or in another class, look up some online shopping, play a game”.

While personally owned internet-connected device use has become the default in most Australian high school classrooms, how and how often they are used is, in fact, the prerogative of the principal. In Queensland, NSW and Victoria principals are required to consult with the school community before setting device policies.

It’s a freedom Pasi Sahlberg, a professor in educational leadership at the University of Melbourne, believes isn’t utilised well enough.

Sahlberg believes that blanket bans such as Victoria’s incoming guidelines reinforce the notion that education professionals cannot be trusted to determine what is best for their students. He would like to see more principals consult with their school’s staff, families and especially students in order to arrive at bespoke policies that best serve their students.

In regional Victoria, principal Justin Hird has done just that. This year he eliminated Castlemaine Secondary College’s longstanding BYOD policy for year 7 students. After getting an “overwhelmingly positive” response from staff, Hird took his proposal to the school community.

He says 98% of all parents were in favour of replacing personal devices with school sets that are only used for specific learning outcomes at school, and not taken home. Hird says consultation with staff suggested removing personal devices from classrooms was a “no brainer”.

While in the minority, Castlemaine secondary joins high schools such as Ashfield Boys high school, Waverley College in Sydney and Traralgon College in regional Victoria in purposefully and substantially limiting the amount of time their students spend on personal screens.

“[Teachers] were experiencing it first-hand in the classroom; the distractions, the students being unable to self-regulate,” Hird says. “It was taking up a lot of time and energy and they felt they were losing quality teaching time because of this distraction.

“There is definitely a place for digital technologies, but it needs to be purposeful and really structured, using specific programs that are going to improve outcomes in particular areas.”

Hird says parents have reported that kids are spending less time on screens at home (compared to older siblings that have personal laptops) and at school he says staff have reported better social interactions among the cohort. Next year the policy will expand to years 8 and 9.

At Sydney Grammar private school, one of the country’s oldest, elite educational institutions, there has never been a BYOD program. Headmaster Stuart McPherson says that while school-owned devices are occasionally used “there’ll be no devices in the average classroom on an average day”.

Like his predecessor, Dr John Valant, McPherson is a firm believer that the foundation of education is human interaction. “Technology has lots of distractions. And that seemed pretty obvious from the beginning. But we don’t want distraction, we want concentration.”

McPherson says that while he appreciates the opportunities technology has to offer in specific circumstances, he regularly reminds students that “knowledge matters and there’s no substitute for it”.

It’s a conviction Jane says often falls on deaf ears in her own classrooms. She believes years of skimming websites, copying and pasting “and making PowerPoints” have left many students unable to analyse texts, or “really think for themselves at all”.

“So I have to go back and teach them how to read critically, and how to decipher and how to form opinions.”

Jane insists her students work from hard copies. “And at the end of it, I ask, do you prefer this to looking at a screen? Absolutely, they say.”

title: Fairphone 6+ review: the most repairable, ethical phone gets faster
description:

fullText:
Dutch sustainable smartphone revamped with new chip and more RAM without sacrificing modular design

Fairphone’s top Android for 2026 is a little faster with more memory while maintaining full compatibility with its previous phone, including its repairable and ethical chops.

The Fairphone 6+ continues the Dutch cooperative’s mission to make consumer electronics longer lasting and more sustainable, containing 51% either recycled or ethically sourced materials while being fully repairable at home with just the one screwdriver included in the box.

It is also the first model to expand beyond Europe, going on sale in the US directly from Fairphone. But the new Android costs £70 (€50) more than the launch price of its predecessor, available from £569 (€649/$650), competing directly with Google’s £499 Pixel 10a and Apple’s £599 iPhone 17e.

The 6+ is an almost exact clone of the Fairphone 6, with the same plastic body, 120Hz OLED screen and fingerprint scanner in the power button. It also supports the same excellent modular accessories that simply screw into the back of the phone to add a lanyard, handle or wallet.

The new model is 2g heavier, but the biggest difference for the 6+ is an upgraded chip to the newer Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 and an additional 4GB of memory for 12GB in total.

The Gen 4 chip is about six to 10% faster in testing, which places it firmly in the mid-range category alongside the likes of the Nothing Phone 4a Pro with the same chip. It won’t win any performance awards and is significantly slower than chips used in Apple, Samsung or Google’s latest smartphones, but it feels snappy enough in use and can be used for light gaming without issue.

The battery life is very similar to the phone’s predecessor, lasting about a day and a half between charges with the screen actively used for about five hours across 5G and wifi, for messaging, note-taking, photos and browsing. Most will need to charge it nightly, which is a bit behind the curve. A full charge takes about 80 minutes using a 30W power adaptor (not included), hitting 50% in under half an hour.

The 6+ also has the same dual-camera system as its predecessor with a 50-megapixel main and 13MP ultra-wide camera. It has improved since its debut last year through software updates, which have fixed a few of the issues and inconsistencies. It can shoot pretty good photos with a bit of work and manages a reasonable 2x zoom. It isn’t the best in lower light conditions, though its new Super Night AI feature helps.

Screen: 6.31in 120Hz FHD+ OLED (431ppi)

Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 4

Camera: 50MP + 13MP, 32MP selfie

Connectivity: 5G, eSIM, wifi 6E, NFC, Bluetooth 5.4 and GNSS

Water resistance: IP55 (splash/rain)

Dimensions: 156.6 x 73.3 x 9.6mm

The 6+ ships with last year’s Android 16, not the latest Android 17, but will be supported with updates until 2033 at least, which is roughly the same as mainstream rivals.

Fairphone’s software is generally clean and uncluttered with only an additional gallery app and the My Fairphone app for repair and diagnostics from the standard Android app loadout. It has Google’s Gemini in various bits, but no other AI additions to get in the way. It also features Fairphone’s “Moments” minimalist interface, activated by the big yellow switch on the side, for a less distracting smartphone experience.

But for those who want an alternative to Google’s Android, the phone is available with the privacy-focused, open-source version of Android, without Google services, called /e/OS.

The battery will maintain at least 80% of its original capacity for 1,000 full charge cycles and it can be replaced at home using a single screwdriver along with the rest of the 12 modular components. Batteries cost £34.20, screens £77.00 and the main camera £59.88. The phone was awarded 10 out of 10 for repairability by specialists iFixit.

The handset is made with 51% recycled or fair materials, while Fairphone publishes life cycle reports for its products.

The Fairphone Gen 6+ costs £569 (€649/$649.99) with Google Android or £598.63 (€699.99/$699.99) with e/OS.

For comparison, the Google Pixel 10a costs £499, the Apple iPhone 17e costs £599 and the Nothing Phone 4a Pro costs £519.

The Fairphone 6+ continues to demonstrate that good, solid Android phones can be made fully repairable at home without specialist tools.

It is only a small spec bump on the original Fairphone 6, which helps keep up with mainstream rivals without sacrificing parts compatibility, sustainability or ethical credentials. It is also available directly in the US for the first time. But that also means the 6+ shares the same flaws as its predecessor.

The camera, battery life, performance and screen are all decent, if far from the best you can get for the money. However, those looking for a high-end smartphone experience best look elsewhere as the Fairphone can’t match a recent iPhone, Pixel or Galaxy S with similar levels of software support.

That makes it hard to recommend to everyone. But for those who prioritise repairability and ethical ethos, this is the phone for you.

Pros: choice of Android operating systems, modular accessories, repairable-at-home design, recycled and fair materials, microSD card slot, good screen, five-year warranty, software support to 2033

Cons: mid-range performance, average battery life, fingerprint scanner can be tricky to press, average camera, cannot be submerged in water, no Android 17 yet.

title: It’s ‘Black August’ in Russia, but Putin is sweeping this summer’s crisis under the rug
description: “Black August,” or “the August curse,” has become a sort of journalistic shorthand in Russia for dramatic crises that seem to happen in the last weeks of summer. But amid the uneasy speculation this y...
fullText:
Over the past few decades, "Black August," or "the August curse," has become a sort of journalistic shorthand in Russia for dramatic crises that seem to happen in the last weeks of summer.

In some respects, Black August is Russia's rough equivalent to the "silly season" in British journalism, the late-summer lull when frivolous headlines seem to dominate while parliament is out of session and royals are on holiday – or announce surprise returns home. But Russian folk wisdom is more pessimistic: a scan of recent Russian history appears to support the belief that dramatic, Black Swan events do tend to strike in August.

Thirty-five years ago, a group of Communist hardliners led a failed putsch against Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, unleashing the centrifugal forces that ultimately led to the collapse of the Soviet Union. In August 1998, a financial crisis hit Russia, causing a default on domestic debt and a collapse of the ruble. And one year later, a group of militants led an incursion into the southern Russian republic of Dagestan, kicking off the second Chechen War, a conflict that launched a political unknown, a former KGB officer named Vladimir Putin, into the top echelon of power.

Putin became Russian leader on New Year's Eve of 1999, after a surprise handover by President Boris Yeltsin. But the new tough-guy leader was not immune from the August Curse either. One of his first major tests in office was the sinking of the Kursk, a nuclear submarine that went down with 118 sailors on board. And in August 2008, Russia went to war with neighboring Georgia, showing the belligerent new face of Putin's foreign policy.

The past summer in Russia has also been shaping up as a bleak season for Putin's Russia. Progress on the contested front lines in Ukraine by Russian troops has been scant; the skies over Russian cities have been blackened by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and Amazon-style distribution centers; and long lines at the fuel pumps and rumors of a fresh wave of mobilization have Russians grumbling.

Exiled Russian commentator Ilya Varlamov posted his thoughts on that question this week, saying recurring historical disasters in August were "a coincidence, of course."

But, Varlamov continued, "many Russians await August with apprehension. Especially now, when the country is truly in crisis. … The fuel crisis has returned, prices are rising and have no intention of stopping, the ruble is falling, elections are coming and God knows what else."

Varlamov also noted the recently publicized remarks made by a top Russian economist, who warned that Moscow was facing a "social crisis" and "losing both the technological and economic competition globally" and would not win a war of attrition against a Ukraine backed by the West.

Even loyal, pro-Kremlin tabloid Moskovsky Komsomolets noted the traditional August anxieties in Russia, though it turned to astrology for guidance. "A lunar eclipse is set to occur this month; while not the most massive one, it will take place opposite Pluto – a planet associated with catastrophes," the article read.

"This could trigger social shifts, political changes in relations with neighbors, and domestic unrest. Incidents of accidents, heightened anxiety, and breakdowns – including nervous disorders – may increase."

But amid the uneasy speculation, Putin has projected his usual aura of confidence.

In remarks Wednesday on infrastructure and development projects, the Kremlin leader acknowledged the economic damage inflicted by Ukraine by strikes on the warehouses of e-commerce giant Wildberries, without naming the company – but downplayed their long-term impact.

"It goes without saying that these attacks will not have, do not cause and cannot bring about any critical consequences," he said. "True, they do cause harm – this much is obvious, and we understand this, we see this, and we are aware of it."

The Russian president said those logistics facilities would be built back with government support. But the war in Ukraine has been coming ever closer to home for many Russians, hitting them squarely in the pocketbooks.

Ukraine is also weathering domestic crisis in wartime. Earlier this week, recently ousted Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for wartime elections, presenting a fresh political challenge to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Whatever the merits of Fedorov's arguments, the move potentially presents a fresh talking point to Putin, who has publicly and repeatedly cast doubt on Zelensky's legitimacy as president.

Zelensky's five-year term was originally expected to end in 2024, but elections in Ukraine have been postponed under martial law imposed following Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. And the government reshuffles in Kyiv, as well as major anti-government protests, show that civil society and democratic processes are still alive and well in Ukraine.

The same can hardly be said for Russia. On Monday, a court in that country convicted opposition politician Lev Shlosberg to 11 years in prison for opposing the war in Ukraine Russia's Supreme Court also barred Shlosberg's party, Yabloko, from appearing on the ballot in upcoming parliamentary elections.

Russia's domestic political opposition, then, has been effectively throttled since Putin launched his war on Ukraine. As the American author Ernest Hemingway would doubtless recognize, the stifling of civil society seemed to happen slowly, then all at once with the death of jailed opposition leader Alexey Navalny in February 2024. Navalny's fatal journey to an Arctic prison colony also began on an August day in 2020, when he fell ill from nerve-agent poisoning on a return flight to Moscow from Siberia.

Coincidence or not, the month of August has been a punishing one for Russia.

title: Virginia Dem admits system ‘failure’ after illegal immigrant accused in landlord killing escapes to Tajikistan
description: Northern Virginia Democrats Donald Beyer and Suhas Subramanyam faced questions after a Tajik national fled a mental health institute to Dushanbe.
fullText:
Northern Virginia Democrats faced questions about how a Tajik national committed to a psychiatric facility after killing his landlord was twice allowed to leave — once to obtain a passport and once to visit an apartment — before escaping to Tajikistan.

Abdulloi Doniyor Toshpulodzoda had been held at a mental health facility in Falls Church, Virginia, after being found not guilty by reason of insanity in the killing of his landlord but was allowed an escorted visit to the Tajik embassy in Foggy Bottom, DC, and later to an Alexandria apartment, where he obtained an airline ticket to Dushanbe and left the country.

"I don't know about investigation, but certainly it's a bad thing that he's not in our custody, not being subject to the laws of the United States," Rep. Donald Beyer, D-Va., told Fox News Digital when asked if federal authorities should investigate the situation.

"There's a failure in the system somewhere along the way. I don't know whether it's failure to put [Toshpulodzoda] in the mental hospital or the hospital didn't have the right security to keep them there. But no, we don't want bad guys on the loose," Beyer said. His district includes Alexandria, Arlington and part of Fairfax County, including the Northern Virginia Mental Health Institute, where Toshpulodzoda was housed.

Beyer pushed back on criticism of Fairfax County, saying he does not believe local leaders would consider it a "sanctuary" jurisdiction for illegal immigrants. He also said he presumed Fairfax County Commonwealth's Attorney Steve Descano was justified in having Toshpulodzoda committed to the psychiatric facility.

Beyer also pushed back on arguments that Toshpulodzoda should have been deported rather than committed to a psychiatric facility, saying someone who commits a serious crime should face consequences in the U.S. before being sent home.

"Deportation doesn't seem sufficient punishment for someone who's [committed] a major felony," Beyer said.

Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, who represents neighboring Loudoun and Fauquier counties, told Fox News Digital that U.S. laws cover murder and violent crime and that criminals "should be held accountable."

"I've been pretty consistent that if someone's undocumented and they committed a crime, that they should be held accountable for the crime and we should look into whether they should be deported at that point," Subramanyam, a Democrat, said.

"So you know, I think that's the federal law at this point and we have to go case by case though, because not every person who commits any crime should be deported automatically, right."

Subramanyam said officials should consider the circumstances when illegal immigrants commit minor offenses such as moving violations while also verifying a suspect's immigration status.

"We have to make sure we go case by case, but. In the instance of violent crime, for instance, they need to be held accountable," he said.

"I want to make sure that if an ICE officer does the wrong thing that they're held accountable and there's not a cover up for them… that's what happened in the case of Renee Good was that a lot of public pressure led to some people getting removed, but that wasn't enough when they need to actually have the DOJ and FBI investigate and prosecute instances where they're going too far."

Good, an anti-ICE activist in Minnesota, was shot and killed by an ICE agent in January after officials said she tried to strike him with her car while shadowing immigration enforcement operations.

Laura Birnbaum, a spokesperson for Descano, told Fox News Digital that the office did not oppose Toshpulodzoda's escorted visit to the embassy in 2024 but has successfully argued multiple times in court against his outright release.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Tajik embassy for comment.

title: The gay rugby player who feared rejection but got total support
description: Kyle Tayler-Woolston feared rejection as a gay man in rugby, but is flourishing in Super Rygbi Cymru thanks to the support at Newport.
fullText:
It will be business as usual for Kyle Tayler with Newport in Super Rygbi Cymru (SRC) this season, the only change will be that he has a different name.

The open-side flanker goes into 2026-27 with the addition of Woolston after his summer wedding to husband George.

The Black and Ambers marked the occasion – the first same-sex blessing held at St Basil's Church in Bassaleg – with a post on social media.

It was another step for a back-row forward who has been "out" with his team-mates since 2018.

"Everyone has been really supportive," said Tayler-Woolston.

"I'd love to give people confidence that there are happy stories out there.

"There are a lot of young players in our squad and when I was in their situation, I didn't have a role model to look up to.

"I know I have the support of Newport – the squad, coaches, committee, fans."

Welsh rugby has high-profile gay men in Gareth Thomas and Nigel Owens, but Tayler-Woolston hopes his experience at semi-professional level will reassure others that they can be themselves.

Wales pushing the pain barrier in bid to improve

'Borderline Personality Disorder is my superpower'

High court allows rugby brain injury case to go on

Tayler-Woolston grew up watching Newport with his father, Andrew, and was treated to a side that featured South Africa internationals Gary Tiechmann and Percy Montgomery in the pre-regional era.

After captaining Cardiff Met and Wales Students then playing for Newbridge, he got the chance to pull on a black and amber jersey for the first time against Cardiff on permit in October 2015.

A permanent move followed, but the flanker was unable to be at his best.

Tayler-Woolston came out to his family in his late teens – "I couldn't have asked for a better reaction from my parents, they weren't bothered at all" – but kept secrets in rugby settings.

"I was sort of living a double life, and then you are lying to yourself," he said.

"My biggest worry was that I would be judged based on my sexuality rather than my rugby skill.

"I think it was my second year with Newport that I started to think that I had to tell people, that I couldn't bottle things up any more.

"It was mentally draining and I was constantly on guard. I wanted to go to dinner with my partner, I wanted to hold their hand without constantly looking over my shoulder."

Relatively new in the squad, Tayler-Woolston's biggest fear was being rejected.

He wondered how the coaching staff react, and whether they would continue to pick him?

"All those ideas were building in my head because you read horror stories online," he added.

"I felt that I was lying to my team-mates because I couldn't be my true, authentic self around them.

"It is tiring being on guard all of the time, wondering what people would think, whether I would be isolated and rejected.

"I love pulling on the black and amber jersey, I never take it for granted and it means so much.

"It would have been devastating to be rejected by my club and city, but thankfully I've never faced that."

Tayler-Woolston gradually told a select few at the club about his sexuality, but needed to tell his boss, head coach Ty Morris.

"He had signed me and invested in me – I owed it to him," he said.

"I messaged Ty and said I had something I needed to tell him and we met for a coffee.

"I just came out and said it and he just said 'oh my god, I thought you were going to tell me you were signing for someone else'.

"Ty was amazing, he has been so supportive and is one of the reasons that I have had such longevity at the club.

"I wanted to be assessed on my rugby, and Ty has always done that. If my performance is rubbish then drop me, and he does. That's down to how I have played and nothing else.

"My biggest fear was the line being blurred, but I don't have to worry about that and can focus on my rugby."

At that cafe summit, the flanker talked through the next steps with Morris and let his news spread naturally through the squad and management with no issues, only encouragement.

"In my head, and I don't know where I got it from, I thought the older generation in rugby would be homophobic, but they weren't," said Tayler-Woolston.

"It's shown me how important it is not to put people in a box and think they will not accept you."

The 2018-19 season was pretty ordinary for Newport, who finished seventh in a 16-team Premiership, but it was a stellar one for Tayler-Woolston.

The flanker swept the board at the Black and Ambers' awards when named as player of the season by his team-mates, the coaches and supporters.

Tayler was being helped by the influence of his future husband, a wedding planner from Bristol.

"That was the first full year that George was coming to games and I was openly talking about my sexuality," he said.

"A weight was off my shoulders, I could be myself and it was reflected in the performances. I wasn't worried about small things.

"Before it was really uncomfortable when I came off the pitch – do I hug him? Do I kiss him? He gave me the confidence to not care what people might think."

Tayler-Woolston is quick to stress that he is lucky with how things have worked out; while offering others encouragement, he certainly isn't preaching.

"I have never faced homophobia in the rugby setting. Maybe that's just because I've been lucky or it's the standard that I am playing at," he said.

"We've had boys in the squad from all walks of life and there has never been an issue, nobody saying that they aren't going to pass to me, talk to me, get changed in front me.

"I've been very lucky, I've got gay friends and some of the battles that they have had, in and out of rugby, are scary.

"I love publicising the fact that you can be open in rugby, but it's someone's own decision."

Tayler-Woolston started in Newport's 2025 Super Rygbi Cymru grand final win at Ebbw Vale and in last season's SRC Cup final success against Llandovery.

He has made 176 appearances for the club and is established as a stalwart, with a big target remaining.

"It'd be a dream to reach 200 if my body can hold out," he said.

"I've managed to achieve everything a semi-pro player can – we've won the cup, the league and we've got the SRC Shield at the moment – all while being open about who I am.

"I do feel rugby has progressed massively and I am able to live my normal life, and that's how it should be, but we have to keep breaking down barriers.

"People shouldn't need to have personal battles, they should be able to go into any rugby club and be themselves. Love is love."

title: The Treasury’s recent moves in the bond and currency markets add up to ‘soft-form financial repression’ to lower debt costs, economist warns
description: "If the market price of USTs is not 'allowed' to adjust down, the foreign exchange price of UST owned by foreign investors has to adjust via a weakening in the dollar."
fullText:
With U.S. debt hitting $40 trillion, markets are turning more attention to that burden and whether policymakers will address the root causes or just the symptoms.

The Treasury Department's interventions in the bond and currency markets in recent weeks point to the latter.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent surprised Wall Street on Wednesday with a plan to increase buybacks of long-term bonds, after the 30-year yield hit the highest level in nearly 20 years.

That came just a few weeks after the U.S. and Japan took such joint action to boost the yen for the first time in three decades. But to make it happen, the U.S. sold euros instead of dollar-denominated assets, avoiding a sale of Treasury securities that would put more upward pressure on yields.

Japan also refrained from selling Treasuries and instead tapped an obscure Federal Reserve tool called the Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility (FIMA). This mechanism allowed Japan, which is the world's largest holder of U.S. debt, to borrow dollars against its Treasury stockpile, obtaining a limited form of liquidity.

According to George Saravelos, head of FX research at Deutsche Bank, "we see both the buyback and encouragement to use the FIMA facility for FX reserves as soft-form financial repression policies aimed at containing the long-end of the US yield curve."

Financial repression generally refers to policies that enable a government to keep interest rates artificially low by influencing financial markets.

Countries throughout history have practiced it, especially during times of high indebtedness. In fact, the U.S. and other developed economies used financial repression to slash their debt-to-GDP ratios after World War II.

Indeed, conflict and calamities are major factors in financial repression. A recent survey of 300 years of U.S. and U.K. history found that wars are "always disaster times" for holders of government debt because of inflation and financial repression.

It's not good for currencies either. Saravelos warned that suppressing U.S. Treasury yields will merely shift the impact to the dollar.

"If the market price of USTs is not 'allowed' to adjust down, the foreign exchange price of UST owned by foreign investors has to adjust via a weakening in the dollar," he explained.

Markets will next scrutinize how the Federal Reserve responds, Saravelos predicted, pointing out that Bessent's moves to effectively loosen financial conditions would typically prompt the Fed to offset that with tightening measures.

title: Sean Grayson, former Illinois deputy convicted of killing Sonya Massey, dies in prison, lawyer says
description: — Sean Grayson, a former Illinois sheriff’s deputy whose fatal shooting of Sonya Massey inside her home became a flashpoint over police use of force, died Sunday while serving a 20-year p...
fullText:
Sean Grayson, a former Illinois sheriff's deputy whose fatal shooting of Sonya Massey inside her home became a flashpoint over police use of force, died Sunday while serving a 20-year prison sentence.

Grayson's attorney, Daniel Fultz, confirmed that his client died earlier Sunday but declined to provide any further details.

Grayson, 32, was convicted of second-degree murder in October in the fatal shooting of Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman who had reported a possible prowler outside her Springfield-area home. Body camera video of the July 2024 encounter showed Massey crouching in her kitchen and apologizing moments before Grayson shot her in the face.

He was sentenced in January to the maximum 20 years in prison.

Grayson had been diagnosed with colon cancer before Massey's killing, and his attorneys said at his sentencing that the disease had spread to his liver and lungs. In May, only months into his sentence, he sought medical release under an Illinois law for prisoners with terminal illnesses or serious medical conditions. The Illinois Prisoner Review Board denied his request last month.

Massey called 911 early on July 6, 2024, to report someone prowling outside her home. Grayson and another Sangamon County sheriff's deputy responded.

Video showed Grayson directing Massey to remove a pot of hot water from the stove. As she held the pot, Massey told the deputies, "I rebuke you in the name of Jesus."

Grayson threatened to shoot her, drew his handgun and ordered her to drop the pot. Massey apologized and ducked behind a kitchen counter before Grayson fired three times.

The other deputy, Dawson Farley, later testified that he did not consider Massey a threat and drew his own weapon only after Grayson did.

Grayson was fired after the shooting and charged with first-degree murder. Jurors convicted him of the lesser charge of second-degree murder after Grayson argued that he feared Massey would throw the hot water at him.

Massey's killing drew national attention and protests and raised questions about how Grayson had moved through several law enforcement agencies before being hired by the Sangamon County Sheriff's Office.

Illinois lawmakers later passed the Sonya Massey Act, requiring law enforcement agencies to more closely review an applicant's previous employment records before hiring an officer.

The Justice Department also opened a civil rights investigation after Massey's death and later reached an agreement with Sangamon County, its sheriff's office and other agencies requiring changes to policing and emergency response. Those changes included additional training for interactions with people with behavioral health disabilities and development of a mobile crisis response program.

NEW YORK, Aug 23 (Reuters) - Tens of thousands of people have been evacuated this weekend from ‌the area of Reno, Nevada, and many others were under orders to leave ‌on Sunday as a wildfire reached the outskirts of the state's third-most-populous city.

About 42,000 residents have been displaced ​or are in active evacuations with an additional 45,000 in "be prepared to evacuate" status as the Hawk Fire threatened northern Reno, local officials said late Sunday morning.

Local TV footage showed flames approaching roads. In eyewitness video verified by Reuters, smoke from the hills billowed over nearby residential ‌neighborhoods.

Fire-tracking websites showed evacuation zones extending ⁠from the Sierra Nevada hills to the University of Nevada in northwest Reno.

The fire has burned 13,000 acres (5,261 hectares) so far, officials said ⁠at a press conference on Sunday. The fire was human-caused and remains under investigation, they said.

Three civilians and three first responders have been injured, said Shane Akerson, a commander leading fire and rescue ​operations.

Officials ​first received reports of a fire off Hawk ​Meadow Trail at about 11:15 a.m. ‌PDT (1815 GMT) on Saturday, said Richard Edwards, chief of Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District. Firefighters on Saturday worked amid "extreme red flag conditions," he said.

Red flag conditions are a combination of warm temperatures, very low humidity and strong winds that raise the risk of wildfires.

"We expect those same strong conditions to come back this afternoon," Edwards said on Sunday.

Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo ‌declared a state of emergency late Saturday in ​Washoe County, which includes Reno and parts of Lake ​Tahoe.

"This is an active and rapidly evolving ​situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain ‌vigilant and follow the direction of local ​officials," Lombardo said in ​a statement.

Lombardo authorized the deployment of two National Guard helicopters to help fight fires and 60 National Guard personnel to support operations with the Washoe County Sheriff's Office, ​officials said.

The Reno-Tahoe International Airport ‌remained outside the evacuation area, and commercial flights were operating normally on Sunday.

(Reporting ​by Siddharth Cavale in New York and Suzanne McGee in Providence, Rhode ​Island; Editing by Sergio Non and Mark Porter)

title: Minnesota tree trimmer charged in coworker’s death after on-the-job horseplay turns deadly
description: A Minnesota tree-trimming employee faces a manslaughter charge after allegedly crushing his coworker’s head with a hydraulic grapple.
fullText:
A tree-trimming employee has been charged with manslaughter after allegedly crushing his coworker's head with a hydraulic grapple while the pair were reportedly "f—ing around" on the job, according to Minnesota authorities.

The incident happened in Apple Valley on Thursday when Christopher Boone Crimmins, 34, was operating machinery on the back of a truck while his coworker, Tyler Anthony Lynch, 26, was on the ground cleaning up branches, according to a criminal complaint filed by Dakota County.

Responding to reports of an incident, police discovered Lynch lying on the ground with "a significant amount of blood around him and significant trauma to his head," the complaint said.

Lynch was pronounced dead at the scene, according to the county.

Workers Warned Ohio Trench Was Too Deep But Were Told To Enter Minutes Before Fatal Cave-in: Report

Authorities said Crimmins was operating a boom, a movable mechanical arm attached to a truck, when he and Lynch began messing around with their shadows.

"He and the Victim were 'f—ing around' and saw that the sunlight was casting shadows of both the grapple and of the Victim on the street," the criminal complaint said.

While looking at the shadows, Crimmins allegedly maneuvered the grapple so that its shadow appeared to grab Lynch's shadow.

However, he did not realize that the grapple itself was moving toward Lynch's head.

Two Workers Killed, Several Injured After Explosions Tear Through Ohio Recycling Facility

"Crimmins was not monitoring the actual grapple or Lynch. He then opened and closed the grapple, crushing Lynch's head," the Dakota County Attorney's Office said.

A witness also saw the incident unfold and said the grapple appeared to "hit or pinch" Lynch's head as it approached him.

Officers observed blood on the grapple, which was directly above Lynch, according to the complaint.

Authorities alleged Crimmins was responsible for the incident through negligence, saying he created an "unreasonable risk" and "consciously takes chances of causing death or great bodily harm to another."

Crimmins has been charged with one felony count of second-degree manslaughter. If convicted, he faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a $20,000 fine.

Officials said Crimmins was being held at the Dakota County Jail. Bail was set at $40,000 without conditions or $20,000 with conditions.

title: Infantino must remember he is European - Ceferin
description: Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin says his Fifa counterpart Gianni Infantino's attempt to sell off a stake in the World Cup was "worse than the Super League".
fullText:
Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin says Gianni Infantino needs to remember he is European after describing his Fifa counterpart's plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup as "worse than the Super League".

Earlier this month the world governing body abandoned Infantino's proposal to create a new company - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) - to manage the commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, with 21% to be sold off to a private investment company.

Uefa led opposition to the plan, with its members voting to boycott World Cups unless it was scrapped.

European football's governing body has since said it has lost confidence in Infantino, while the football associations of all the home nations have withdrawn support for the 56-year-old Swiss.

"I think this plan is even worse than the Super League plan," Ceferin told the Rest is Politics podcast., external

"Super important clubs wanted to do their own league, which is wrong, and would destroy football. But in this case, football would be literally sold.

"I'm absolutely sure that the plan is dead. It's hard to to imagine what kind of people would sell the sport that belongs to everyone. We will not allow that to happen."

The European Super League was a proposed breakaway league of 20 top European clubs as a rival to Uefa's Champions League, but the project fell apart days after its unveiling in April 2021 after widespread criticism.

Ceferin said that Uefa had no prior knowledge of Infantino's plan, and that he found out through the media while on holiday with his family.

"He didn't contact me since this happened," Ceferin said.

"They [Fifa] play on, you know, '[how] arrogant Europe is against us: They have enough money, but I help the small and the poor'.

"But I think someone should remind him that he is a European, and that he was supported by Uefa, which he forgot."

Infantino - who worked at Uefa for 16 years, and was general secretary for nine - has been flying around the world in the search of public support.

On Saturday, he met with Caribbean Football Union members in the Dominican Republic and on Sunday he was at the E-Sports World Cup in Paris, attended by the French President Emmanuel Macron, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Portugal forward Cristiano Ronaldo.

Infantino asked to stay away from youth tournament

Scottish FA withdraws support for Fifa president Infantino

Ceferin confirmed he would not run to become Fifa president at the Fifa Congress in March 2027, when Infantino will look to secure a fourth term in the role.

"I'm not interested because of two reasons. One reason is that I love Uefa and I love working here, and I think that at a certain point it's time also to enjoy life a bit," the 58-year-old Slovenian said.

"And the second point is, my credibility is much, much, much higher if I'm not interested in the position."

Before his aborted FFE proposal, Infantino was coming under increasing pressure over his relationship with United States President Donald Trump.

After US striker Folarin Balogun had a red card suspension overturned so that he could play in his side's defeat by Belgium in the last 16 of this summer's World Cup, Trump revealed he personally called Infantino to request the sanction be lifted.

Earlier this month, Trump said it would be a "terrible mistake" to remove Infantino as Fifa president.

"That was more than shocking. We have rules, and if you don't respect your own rules, then the game doesn't make any sense," Ceferin said on the incident.

"The president of a country says: 'I called him, and I told him to look at it.' And then the Fifa president says it was an independent decision.

"I mean, for us as football fans, or for us as a governing body, that's shocking. That's shocking, and - trust me - almost everybody was shocked. Just not everybody dared to speak."

title: The maths whizz turned £86m teenage star heading to Man City
description: Manchester City have agreed a deal in principle with Lille to sign midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi - what makes him such a highly rated talent?
fullText:
Olivier Giroud knows a prodigious talent when he sees one.

"I played with Kylian Mbappe when he was 18," the Lille striker said. "He was so mature for his age and I have the same feeling with Ayyoub."

But the teenage Moroccan's "rise to prominence is nothing new" in the words of another club insider.

The manner in which the midfielder impressed at the World Cup did not come as a surprise to anyone in Creil, either, where the 18-year-old grew up in northern France.

"No one is shocked here," said his former coach Sofiane Khair. "For us, it's logical."

Now, Bouaddi is on his way to the Premier League, with Manchester City agreeing a deal worth 100m euros (£86m) in principle to sign him from Lille.

Bouaddi is not just in demand at club level - Morocco and France also both desperately wanted him.

Giroud, a World Cup winner, was in his ear, "teasing him the whole year regarding picking France".

Bouaddi may have represented Les Bleus throughout the youth age groups, but he has always been immensely proud of his family's roots.

Explaining his ultimate decision to declare for Morocco, rather than the country of his birth, Bouaddi uploaded an old photograph on Instagram.

It captured the then 10-year-old in a Morocco shirt as he watched on from the stands at the 2018 World Cup.

"I am aware of the privilege I have to defend these colours and I will give everything to best represent my country," he vowed.

Bouaddi certainly backed up those words as Morocco became the first African nation to reach successive World Cup quarter-finals.

"Against players like Casemiro, Lucas Paqueta and Bruno Guimaraes, he showed not just quality but personality - a kind of positive arrogance," former Morocco international Hassan Kachloul told BBC Sport.

"He had confidence, a great aura and a strong presence on the pitch. He thrives in that environment."

However, to those who know Bouaddi best, such as former Creil coach Armand Doue, his performances were nothing out of the ordinary.

"He does this kind of match every weekend on the pitches of Ligue 1," he said.

Bouaddi's ability to step up in such fashion has been a constant throughout his burgeoning career.

The platform may have been even greater at the World Cup, but the unfazed teenager has relished competing against older players for much of his life.

He became the youngest footballer to ever play for Lille when he made his senior debut against KI just a few days after turning 16 in 2023.

He was serenaded by those inside the Stade Pierre-Mauroy after helping Lille defeat Real Madrid in the Champions League on his 17th birthday.

He then broke a record held by Eden Hazard after making 50 Ligue 1 appearances for Lille at the age of just 18.

It is already quite a CV but what has struck Giroud, in particular, is Bouaddi's willingness to take advice on board.

His "perfect team-mate" knows he is far from the finished article.

"He's a proper box-to-box player, but he needs to improve some things, like his finishing," Giroud said.

Moroccan football journalist Amine el Amri tells BBC Sport the midfielder has the potential to "be one of the best midfielders ever in the game".

"He has such talent but he has to keep his cool and his feet on the ground. You can't be a star if you don't work hard enough," he said.

"At first glance, he reminds you a lot of [former Spain and Barcelona midfielder] Sergio Busquets. He is very tall but also not very muscular. Normally you would get players with muscles in the number six or eight position.

"What he does best is keep his cool when he has the ball and when he is pressing. He doesn't commit a lot of fouls, which is what made Busquets a complete midfielder."

Bouaddi's thirst to improve is a recurring theme and Diop describes him as "a player who always questions himself because he is a perfectionist".

This trait also quickly struck coach Mickael Delestrez when Bouaddi made the jump to Lille's under-17s at the age of 15.

"He's one of those boys who, during his first game playing up an age group, would ask, 'What do you expect from me?'" he said.

"His reflective nature leads to him constantly questioning his game - what could he have done better or what should he have done differently?

"He possesses this analytical ability that allows him to continually challenge himself."

The same is true of his approach to life away from the pitch.

Bouaddi has been studying for a mathematics degree in his spare time and previously won an oratory competition after delivering a speech at Elysee Palace.

He was always a little different.

Coach Khair knows that only too well after seeing Bouaddi take some of his first steps in the game at Creil.

"Ayyoub didn't have a PlayStation or a Nintendo DS," he said. "When he wasn't playing, he stayed at home reading books or doing his homework.

"He never had fast food, either. When we went to tournaments, he was the only kid who did not eat burgers or pizza.

"He's the same now as he was when he was 10."

title: California dad paralyzed from neck down after diving into ocean to rescue child
description: A California father dove into a rip current to save a child at a beach and suffered a spinal cord injury that left him paralyzed from the neck down.
fullText:
A California father of five was paralyzed from the neck down after entering the ocean in an effort to help a young child who his family said was caught in a rip current.

Josh Collette, 42, was spending time with his family at Riviera Beach in San Clemente, California, on Aug. 15, when a child believed to be 7- or 8-years-old became caught in a rip current, the man's sister, Hillary Collette, told KTLA.

The child's mother first entered the water to go after her child, but Josh Collette ran past her and dove into the ocean in an effort to help the child, Hillary Collette told the outlet.

Georgia Teacher, Father Hailed As Hero After Dying To Save Girl From Myrtle Beach Rip Current

As he entered the water, Collette's sister said he struck either a sandbar or rocks and was immediately injured.

Several people then rushed to his aid and helped pull him from the water. He told his wife right away that he believed he had broken his neck.

The child Josh Collette was attempting to help was safely pulled out of the water before Collette was brought from the water, his sister said.

Collette's sister said doctors told the family that Josh Collette was paralyzed from the neck down.

His sister said he was unable to speak but communicated by moving his lips; she said the family expects him to regain his ability to speak.

His family created a GoFundMe as they prepare to help with medical bills, long-term therapy and support for the family as they navigate the long and difficult recovery ahead.

"Josh was hurt in an ocean accident on Sat Aug 15th he has a spinal cord injury," a family member wrote on the fundraiser. "The road ahead will be long, and the recovery will not be easy, we're holding on to hope."

"We believe in miracles! We've already seen so many and thank everyone for the love, support, and prayers!" the fundraiser added. "Please keep praying for miracles! Its working!"

'Hero' Father Drowns Saving His 12-Year-old Son From Rip Current At Popular Beach Destination, Family Says

In an update shared on Friday, the family said it will take some time for him to no longer need medicine. The family also shared a picture of Josh Collette from his hospital bed.

"Yesterday was so positive and productive! So, it was hard to have a day with less progress. This guy hates medicine! He's trying hard to get off of everything... but, that's going to take some time. Thank you so much for all the prayers, love, and support. We love you all so much and feel so loved by all the help you've given us. We're hanging in there and so grateful for all of you," the family wrote on the fundraiser.

The GoFundMe has raised nearly $110,000 as of Sunday night.

title: China probes use of formaldehyde to keep cabbages fresh
description: Using the carcinogen to preserve food is prohibited in China, the world's largest producer of cabbages.
fullText:
Authorities in China have launched an investigation into reports of formaldehyde being used to preserve the freshness of cabbages for human consumption.

Officials in the northeastern Hebei province confirmed that they had verified footage showing individuals dipping cabbages in a solution before loading them onto trucks for transportation.

An environmental blogger first released the footage last week. Using formaldehyde, a colourless chemical that is known to cause cancer, for preserving the freshness of food in China is strictly prohibited.

China is the world's largest producer of cabbages, most of which are exported to neighbouring countries in Asia.

Police have taken legal action against the individuals involved, according to state media.

Officials are now moving swiftly to prevent panic and restore confidence by carrying out spot checks on markets across the country.

Chinese state media says investigators will also establish how widespread the practice is and take measures to trace affected vegetables.

In a statement issued on Saturday, local authorities in Kangbao county said: "Any illegal or non-compliant practices discovered will be dealt with strictly in accordance with the law to ensure the safety of the vegetable supply."

Xinfadi market in Beijing, one of the major sources of fresh produce in the capital, issued a statement saying that it had investigated the source of its cabbages, adding that none of the affected vegetables had entered its market.

The incident has generated widespread media attention in China.

An editorial in the People's Daily wrote: "The wholesalers focused solely on their immediate economic interests while completely disregarding the lives and health of consumers. [They] crossed a legal red line and breached the moral bottom line."

China produces well over 30 million tons of cabbages each year, nearly half of the world's annual total. Vietnam, South Korea and Russia are among the largest export destinations for the vegetable.

Exposure to relatively high quantities of formaldehyde in some workplaces has been linked to some types of cancer in humans, but the effect of exposure to small amounts is less clear, according to the American Cancer Society.
